items.title: US offers $20m reward for information about Iran's nuclear programme
items.summary: Donald Trump has repeatedly raised the prospect of renewing strikes against Iran's nuclear facilities.
items.content:
The US has announced a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran's nuclear programme.
The State Department's Rewards for Justice is also offering to potentially relocate the person who provides such details.
President Donald Trump claimed last year that Iran's nuclear facilities had been "completely and totally obliterated " following a bombing campaign by the US and Israel.
Iran insists its nuclear programme is peaceful and that it has no intention of developing a nuclear weapon.
Meanwhile, the US military says it is setting up a task force to enhance Washington's efforts to restrict Iran's movement of weapons and sanctioned material across its borders.
The US military's Central Command (Centcom) said Task Force Iron Gate would operate from Tampa, Florida, and would work with other US government agencies.
As well as the movement of weapons, it will also focus on dual-use and illegal revenue streams.
Centcom estimates that its naval blockade of Iran's ports has prevented the country from exporting more than $25bn in crude oil.
Major construction ongoing near Iran missile bases, satellite images suggest
A US State Department statement about its multi-million dollar reward said it was offering the money for information about the Iranian programme, including "facilities, equipment and associated personnel".
It said Iran's "lack of compliance with the IAEA [the International Atomic Energy Agency] on safeguards obligations has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components like [nuclear] centrifuges".
Centrifuges are needed to produce enriched uranium, which can be used to make reactor fuel for civilian use but also for nuclear weapons if enriched to around 90% purity or higher.
There had been mounting speculation that the US might resume significant strikes in Iran after the midterm elections, though Trump told reporters, prior to the polls, that he was in "no rush" to do so.
In an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms, the president also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme.
This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump said.
The president has repeatedly threatened to bomb the suspected underground site on previous occasions.
However, both Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have said public opposition to the war on Iran fuelled heavy losses for their Republican Party in this week's midterm elections, which has led to speculation the White House may no longer seek an escalation in the conflict.
On Friday, Trump insisted that Iran was keen to end the eight-month conflict with the US, stressing the damage to Tehran's economy and military.
"We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," he said.
Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said on Tuesday that both sides were "reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented" and that it remained hopeful of a deal being agreed.
Iranian negotiators had discussed with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days once the US met its seven conditions.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Ukraine war briefing: Russia ramping up attacks to ‘pressure’ Kyiv at trilateral talks, Zelenskyy says
President urges US for support, saying ‘Ukraine must not be left to face this alone’ as barrage plunges cities into darkness. What we know on day 1,719
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of intensifying strikes across the country to put pressure on Kyiv at upcoming talks after an overnight barrage triggered power cuts as temperatures drop. “By intensifying its attacks on Ukraine and our infrastructure at this very moment, Russia is trying to additionally lay the groundwork for putting pressure on Ukraine’s position and that of its partners,” the Ukrainian president said. “Russia perceives diplomacy in its own peculiar way – as a form of aggression.”
Ukraine’s energy ministry said “a massive attack on a number of energy facilities” on Saturday had plunged five regions into darkness and significantly hampered electricity transmission in Kyiv and surrounding regions. Russia had throughout the night launched 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy said, among which were KN-23 missiles manufactured and supplied by North Korea.
The strikes came before a US-brokered trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi scheduled for next week aimed at reviving stalled diplomatic efforts towards peace. Ukrainian officials are expected to sit down with Russian negotiators and US envoys on Tuesday and Wednesday for the first such talks in months. The diplomatic track has been stalled since February when Washington shifted attention to its war with Iran.
Zelenskyy also urged the US to increase its flagging aid to Ukraine. “Unfortunately, there is still a significant shortage of interceptors for Patriot systems, and the United States is in the best position to help address it,” he said.
‘My biggest fear was being shot down’: how an injured Ukrainian soldier was evacuated by drone
Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani , on Saturday said he had been targeted by pro-Russian hackers over his backing for Ukraine . Tajani said in a post on X that “backing in a transparent way the freedom and independence of a sovereign state” had made him a target. Tajani said his personal data had been published on the dark web and that the hackers were seeking further information about him and his family and were ‌willing to pay for it.
The Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, who has been one of the strongest backers of Ukraine among western leaders, expressed her support for Tajani and said the sale of confidential information relating to public officials was “a matter of serious concern”. Moscow has not commented ‌on the incident. ‌
France’s far-left presidential contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon said on Saturday that settling the Ukraine conflict could not be done by granting territorial concessions without consulting the people concerned . Melenchon, who polls suggest could reach the second round of next year’s presidential election, set out his France Unbowed party’s foreign policy positions at a rally just outside Paris.
Mélenchon has been criticised in the past for questioning the legitimacy of Zelenskyy. But in a campaign speech to thousands of supporters, he said an administration run by his party would take an active role in settling the war in Ukraine . Europe would have to play an active role in peace talks, he said. “We cannot accept that one could consider a peace with territorial concessions in Ukraine without asking the populations concerned if they agree or not to be on one side or other of the border,” he said. “It is for the people themselves to decide what they want,” he added.
A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia’s Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said on Saturday. Russia’s defence ministry said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov seas, it said. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.

items.content:
Israeli investors warned of AI debt crisis one day before Wall Street’s tech crash
Israeli investors warned of AI debt crisis one day before Wall Street’s tech crash
Senior investment managers warned that debt-fueled AI spending, chip oversupply and S&P 500 concentration were becoming major risks; the next day Nasdaq plunged 5.5%, with Israeli institutions holding tens of billions of shekels in semiconductor exposure
One day before Wall Street suffered one of its steepest selloffs in a year and a half , some of Israel’s most senior investment managers were already warning that the enormous sums pouring into artificial intelligence and technology stocks were creating new risks, with one executive cautioning that the next major crisis could emerge from the debt of technology companies.
Within 24 hours, the risks they had been discussing were suddenly visible on trading screens around the world. On Thursday, the Nasdaq plunged 5.5%, the S&P 500 lost 4.4% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell about 12%. Panic eased on Friday, when the Nasdaq rebounded 1.1% and the S&P 500 gained 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.5%, but the recovery erased only part of the previous day’s losses.
Israeli investors warned of AI debt crisis one day before Wall Street’s tech crash
Tel Aviv also rebounded sharply after the selloff, with the TA-35 jumping 3.09%, the TA-125 rising 2.81% and the banking index climbing 4.52%. The turmoil is particularly significant for Israel’s institutional investors because of their substantial exposure to semiconductors. A Calcalist analysis based on holdings at the end of June 2026 found that Israeli institutions held about 29.3 billion shekels in shares of 10 chip companies, including Nvidia, TSMC, Broadcom and Micron, as well as another 8.4 billion shekels in VanEck’s SMH and iShares’ SOXX semiconductor ETFs. Together, the holdings amount to roughly 37.7 billion shekels, assuming there is no overlap between the datasets, and do not include additional exposure through funds tracking broader indexes such as the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100. Their exposure to Israeli chipmaker Tower Semiconductor alone stood at nearly 19 billion shekels, while Tower shares plunged 12% on Thursday.
Just one day before the market turmoil, senior Israeli investment executives had gathered at a closed conference organized by the country’s Family Office Association, headed by Reuven Titouani, owner of the Talpiot agency. Family offices manage the finances of wealthy families, in some cases overseeing hundreds of millions or billions of shekels, making them an especially attractive audience for insurance companies and investment houses. Representatives from nearly all of Israel’s major institutional investors attended, and two panels focused on equity exposure and, in particular, the risks surrounding U.S. technology stocks. There was no single consensus, but several executives issued significant warnings, and some said they had already begun shifting money from stocks into bonds.
The sharpest warning came from Tamir Hershkovitz, chief investment officer at Ayalon. “It could be that the next major crisis will be a debt crisis among technology companies,” he said. Hershkovitz argued that the huge investments being made in AI infrastructure are increasingly financed through debt and warned that a crisis could develop within two or three years. Technology and semiconductor companies operate in cyclical industries, he noted, meaning today’s enormous investment wave could itself become a source of significant risk if demand fails to match expectations.
Clal Insurance has already begun reducing some of that risk. Barak Bensky, head of its investment division, said the company shifted some money from equities into long-term foreign bonds about a month ago. One of the biggest dangers facing markets, he said, is that the pace of AI investment may fail to meet the lofty expectations already reflected in stock prices. Yotam Eironi, head of foreign equities at Altshuler Shaham, also warned that a slowdown in data-center construction could create excess production capacity for processors and chips in the coming years, making it essential to distinguish between profitable, stable companies and those whose valuations rely heavily on future growth. Migdal executives, meanwhile, highlighted the heavy concentration of the S&P 500. Asked whether savers whose entire pension and long-term savings are invested in an S&P 500 tracking fund should diversify, Maria Yuskovitch replied: “Absolutely. There is room for diversification in investments.”
The pressure was already being felt by Israeli investment managers in local trading. A senior executive at one institutional investor described trading around the latest index update as highly unusual. “It was real madness. Just dump it, just sell,” he told Calcalist. Normally, he said, a steep fall in a stock being removed from an index draws bargain hunters. This time, almost no buyers appeared. “Stocks we held were down 10%, down 15%, and nobody came to buy.” The absence of buyers, he said, only intensified the declines.
Not everyone at the conference was pessimistic. Carmel Kenny of Yelin Lapidot expressed confidence in long-term equity investing, particularly in technology and semiconductor stocks, while stressing the importance of diversification. Yoav Caspi of Phoenix pointed to expected earnings growth among large companies as a reason to continue holding them, while Harel Finance Chief Investment Officer Ronen Kaploto warned against trying to time the market. Raanan Shani of Aspire and Shahaf Buchris of Hachshara also urged investors not to panic over short-term volatility or make hasty portfolio changes.
But the timing gave the warnings unusual weight. Israel’s investment chiefs spent Wednesday debating whether AI spending, semiconductor valuations and heavy concentration in U.S. technology stocks had become dangerous. By Thursday, the Nasdaq was down 5.5%, chip stocks were leading a global selloff and the risks they had described were no longer theoretical.

Why Iran is allowing India, China, Iraq and Qatar to pass through Strait of Hormuz
/ Why Iran is allowing India, China, Iraq and Qatar to pass through Strait of Hormuz
Why Iran is allowing India, China, Iraq and Qatar to pass through Strait of Hormuz
Published: Nov 08, 2026, 16:00 IST | Updated: Nov 08, 2026, 16:55 IST
Ships are anchored off the coast of Khasab in Oman’s Musandam Governorate, near the Strait of Hormuz, on October 2, 2026 Photograph: (AFP)
Iran has allowed India, China, Iraq and Qatar to use the Strait of Hormuz amid its blockade, claiming that it's a transactional relationship.
Since closing the Strait of Hormuz on March 2, following the US-Israeli strike which killed Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other senior leaders, Iran has framed Hormuz as its own geographic weapon to leverage and increase its position as a regional superpower. It has maintained that it is open to everyone except its adversaries. On November 3, Amir Hayat Moqaddam, the deputy chairman of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, confirmed that the Strait is open for India, China, Iraq and Qatar.
"Ships from these countries pass freely, and the Americans do not intercept them either," Amir Hayat Moqaddam, deputy chairman of the Iranian parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, told the Iranian Students' News Agency (ISNA).
Iran's stated reasons are transactional. The Iranian lawmaker who announced the exemptions said India's is meant to facilitate medicine imports into Iran, while China's aims to secure Beijing's political support. Qatar and Iraq are described as "mutual interests." Qatar is also mediating between Tehran and Washington, so favouring it helps keep that channel open. Indian and Chinese ships reportedly pay transit fees, while Qatari ships pass free. In effect, Iran is using access to the strait as currency, rewarding customers, suppliers and mediators while keeping pressure on its adversaries.
Also Read: 'Defeated on battlefield and at ballot box': Iran mocks Trump as CENTCOM announces land blockade
The exemptions help the buyers most reliant on Gulf crude; according to Kpler data, China and India account for 55% of strait crude throughput. But the strait is still far from normal. The EIA estimated that flows averaged 4.9 million barrels a day in Q2 2026, down from 21.6 million in Q4 2025. Selective passage for four countries, with Saudi Arabia left out, doesn't restore that supply. It mostly reshuffles who gets oil and at what cost.

WANA (Nov 08) – Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy has reported the explosion and fire involving a third oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz.
According to a statement by the IRGC Navy’s Public Relations Office, three oil tankers described as violating maritime regulations have suffered explosions and severe fires since the early hours of today while navigating unauthorized routes through the strait. Thick smoke from the fires has reportedly spread across the area.
The statement said the tankers caught fire after switching off their navigation and identification systems and cooperating with what it described as U.S. military operations to pass through unauthorized routes.

items.content:
‘No good options’: Iran war caught between Trump's midterm troubles, Israel's election shake-up
A broader offensive, continued pressure, negotiated compromise, or a limited strike are potential options, according to Raz Zimmt, director of the Iran and the Shiite Axis research program at INSS.
A pedestrian walks past a billboard depicting US President Donald Trump inside a catering container, installed on a building along a street in downtown of Tehran on August 31, 2026.
( photo credit : ATTA KENARE / AFP via Getty Images )
The Democratic victory in the United States midterm elections has reshaped the balance of power in Washington, but it has not resolved the confrontation with Iran. US President Donald Trump still controls the White House, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains in office amid a difficult government-formation process, and Tehran is treating the Republican defeat as evidence that the war has imposed political costs on its adversaries. Whether the new political landscape encourages escalation or negotiation remains uncertain.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The fragility of the situation was demonstrated on Monday, when US forces conducted limited strikes against Iranian targets on Qeshm Island, described by American officials as defensive operations rather than the resumption of major hostilities.
On Thursday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) reported that two oil tankers and a tugboat had caught fire in separate incidents in the Strait of Hormuz, including one tanker allegedly striking a mine. The Iranian account has not been independently verified.
The November 3 vote handed Democrats control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, after a campaign in which the economic consequences of the Iran war became a significant liability for Republicans. But the newly elected Congress will not take office until January 3, 2027. Until then, Republicans retain their existing congressional majorities, and even afterward, Democratic control would not automatically remove the president’s ability to order military action. Congress can contest funding and authorizations, but the scope of presidential war powers remains disputed.
The question is whether another campaign would achieve what previous operations failed to settle or reproduce the same stalemate.
A protester holds a banner opposing the war with Iran during US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's opening remarks at a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on US President Donald Trump's FY2027 budget request for the Department of Defence on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC, US, April 30, 20 (credit: REUTERS/Eric Lee)
For Dr. Nabi Sonboli, a senior expert at Iran’s Institute for Political and International Studies, the central uncertainty is Trump himself. “I prefer not to expect any wise decisions from Trump and his team. Confrontation is still possible,” he told The Media Line.
Sonboli also doubts that congressional opposition could contain an escalation. “The US Congress is not able to control Trump/Netanyahu axis no matter how much costs they impose on the US.”
Dr. Raz Zimmt, director of the Iran and the Shiite Axis research program at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies, sees the US administration confronting a series of imperfect choices. “It's very difficult to assess, first of all, what will be the decision by President Trump,” he told The Media Line. He identified a broader offensive, continued pressure, a negotiated compromise, or a limited strike as potential options.
“One is to continue with his plans to strike Iran. I think he realizes that there are many risks involved in this third round of war against Iran,” Zimmt said. “The second option is to continue with the status quo, putting more pressure on Iran. But again, there is no guarantee that at the end of the day it will convince Iran to offer more concessions.”
Iran unlikely to accept compromises US looking for, analyst says
A diplomatic alternative also faces obstacles. Zimmt said Iran might accept limited concessions concerning the sequence of a possible agreement, but not the substantial compromises Washington seeks. A narrower military option would carry its own danger: even an attack intended to end the confrontation could trigger an Iranian response that prolongs it. “But again, nobody can guarantee that the Iranians will not respond in a way which would escalate things even further,” he said.
“So, what we see currently is that the immediate threat of striking Iran seems to be on hold, both because of the political calculations in the US, but also because of the continued negotiations,” Zimmt said. Limited clashes around the Strait of Hormuz and unresolved disputes over sanctions, shipping, and nuclear activity continue to make escalation possible.
Tehran’s interpretation of the American vote is different. Dr. Ebrahim Roshandel, a former Iranian diplomat and strategic affairs analyst now based in the US, said the election result has prompted the Islamic Republic to strengthen its domestic narrative of resistance. “Now, after this result came from the election, Iranian leader and the IRGC commanders strongly try to change the narrative inside of Iran,” he told The Media Line. “At the same time, it doesn't mean that they are going to open the new door in diplomatic way to negotiate or respond to the United States, because they have some conditions already.”
Roshandel believes Tehran wants Arab states to reassess their reliance on Washington, preferring that they see accommodation with Iran as an alternative. “The first things, I believe, they try to give the message to regional countries, mostly Arab countries, to make a big gap between United States and the Arab countries,” he said.
US soldier after boarding an Iranian ship in the Strait of Hormuz, July 17, 2026. (credit: Screenshot/X/@PeteHegseth)
He also argued that Tehran is attentive to divisions within the administration over the war, naming senior officials whom he believes favor different approaches to negotiations and military force. Those are his interpretations, not verified accounts of the officials’ positions.
Zimmt cautioned that the Republican defeat does not remove the military threat to Iran. “There's no doubt that the Iranians consider the failure, the defeat of the Republicans as a major success, but we still have to remember, and the Iranians realize that, that it doesn't solve the Iranian problem,” he said. “Trump is still very much capable of striking Iran. The Iranians certainly don't want that to happen.”
Israeli election leaves Netanyahu weaker than before
A parallel political uncertainty is unfolding in Israel. The October 27 Knesset election left Netanyahu’s allied parties with 53 of 120 seats, compared with 48 for a bloc associated with opposition figure Gadi Eisenkot . The two Arab-led parties won 19 seats, leaving no obvious governing majority and negotiations over the next government unresolved. Netanyahu continues to lead the country on a caretaker basis, but his political position is weaker than before the vote.
Even so, Zimmt cautioned against assuming that a change of government would fundamentally transform Israel’s assessment of Iran. “Eisenkot might certainly adopt a less hawkish position, but when it comes to the perception in Israel, when it comes to the Iranian threats, the nuclear threat, there is no real difference between Eisenkot and Netanyahu,” he said. “And again, at the end of the day, everyone realizes that the decision is made when it comes to the Iranian file in Washington, not in Jerusalem.”
He was equally direct about Netanyahu’s influence over Trump. “First of all, Netanyahu doesn't make the decisions. With all due respect to Netanyahu, he probably tried to convince President Trump to strike Iran before the elections. He failed to do that, and currently he doesn't have any ability to make Trump do anything,” he said.
On election day, Trump said he and Netanyahu had agreed that Washington would stop providing what he described as $4 billion a year to Israel after the end of 2026. It was unclear which funding he meant or how the change would be implemented. The existing memorandum providing $3.8 billion in annual military assistance runs through September 2028.
Beyond these political changes, Israel’s underlying security concerns remain. Zimmt disputes the idea that missile production should be the principal measure of whether another operation is necessary. “Yes, Iran still has a lot of missile capabilities, but this is not the main problem,” he said. “The main problem right now is that we still have no solution whatsoever to the nuclear capabilities which are still held by Iran.”
He described two unsatisfactory paths: a negotiated agreement that could deliver economic benefits to the Iranian government, or military action that might damage facilities without eliminating the knowledge, equipment, and material associated with the program. The International Atomic Energy Agency has been unable to verify the present location and composition of much of Iran’s enriched-uranium stockpile after losing access to key facilities. The agency estimated that Iran held 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched up to 60% as of June 13, 2025. That enrichment level is far above the level used in ordinary civilian power generation, but it does not establish that Iran possesses a nuclear weapon. The figure is a historical estimate, not a verified measure of the current stockpile.
One proposed target is Pickaxe Mountain , the deeply buried complex near Natanz. Its operational status remains difficult to verify independently. For Zimmt, an aerial attack might delay the site’s use but would not settle the broader nuclear issue.
“It won't deprive Iran from its 440 kilograms of enriched uranium. It's not going to deprive Iran from its hundreds of advanced centrifuges,” he said. “And the only way to deal with the underground tunnels is through special operation, and this is something which is probably not going to happen.”
More ambitious proposals, including strikes against Iranian oil installations and other vital industries, involve a different set of risks. Zimmt said such attacks could severely worsen Iran’s economic crisis and even leave it resembling a failed state, without producing the intended concessions or a change of government. “And so, again, there are no good options right now,” he concluded.
Roshandel’s assessment places greater emphasis on the possibilities for internal political change. He said he has urged the White House to engage with Iranian opposition figures, describing this as an alternative source of leverage. “I remember that in April I sent my third letter to the White House, and I asked President Trump to use other leverage, which is the opposition. But unfortunately, they ignored it,” he said.
He also described domestic weaknesses that military pressure alone cannot resolve: inflation, economic dysfunction, arrests of political activists, and environmental problems. “So, I believe that we will see some breakdown. We will see some huge level of the protest is coming very shortly, maybe in two, three months, we will see that,” he said. He also predicted that the regime could collapse within a year. Zimmt, however, cautioned in a recent analysis that Iran’s deep crises do not make regime change imminent.
The Strait of Hormuz remains both a point of strategic leverage and a potential trigger for renewed conflict. Iranian interference with shipping and the American blockade have aggravated regional uncertainty and energy costs. Gulf states have strong incentives to avoid another exchange that could endanger shipping, oil facilities, or American bases on their territory, even as they remain concerned about Iran’s military capabilities.
Roshandel said Iran would seek concessions from regional governments by emphasizing their dependence on safe passage through the strait. At the same time, he pointed to Qatar as a potentially important intermediary. “My point of view is Qatar has the great potential right now to be more active than before this election to convince both sides to come back to the negotiation,” he said. But he also described Iranian hardliners as demanding sanctions relief, removal of the blockade, and revenge against American officials, a combination that could complicate compromise.
Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani shakes hands with Iranian Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni in Doha, Qatar, October 6, 2026. (credit: Amiri Diwan/Handout via REUTERS)
Diplomatic contacts have already produced a draft proposal. According to Reuters , Iranian negotiators left Doha on Sunday after talks with Qatari mediators. An official briefed on the discussions said their departure was not due to difficulties in the negotiations, that a draft proposal was circulating, and that another meeting was possible. Tehran has linked the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to ending the US naval blockade under a seven-step framework, and Iranian officials have said that implementation could be accelerated to two days if its demands are met. No final agreement has been announced.
Roshandel warned that the consequences of continued confrontation could extend beyond Iran’s borders. “Iran is not going to stop supporting proxy groups, and they are trying to re-emerge or reorganize the new part of the proxies, more operational like Houthis in Yemen. They can make many, many places unstable.” He also expects Tehran to continue supporting aligned armed groups in Iraq and Lebanon.
Russia has also been involved in diplomatic contacts. Russian President Vladimir Putin met Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, in Moscow on Thursday. The Kremlin confirmed the meeting but did not disclose its precise agenda. Zimmt pointed to the encounter as a possible element in wider efforts to avert another confrontation, without claiming that it had produced a breakthrough.
Sonboli, by contrast, emphasized the absence of trust rather than the mechanics of mediation. “Many in Iran expect the war to continue for some time and they have got ready for that,” he said. He argued that Tehran had not sought the war, asserting that: “Peace needs a level of trust and Trump/Netanyahu proved that they are not trustable.”
He also invoked the experience of the George W. Bush administration and the costs of earlier US wars. “That war imposed 5 trillion dollars on the US and there is no reason that we believe the current administration is wiser under Trump,” he concluded.

Risk of Iran war escalation remains high despite Democratic election sweep
Crude oil prices sold off this week as investors hoped the Democratic victory in the U.S. midterm elections would force an end to the Iran war.
But tensions remain high in the Middle East, with the Gulf states still bracing for escalation, analysts say.
The Democrats' options are limited until they take control of Congress in January.
And President Donald Trump has reiterated that he will not allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.
80% odds of renewed military attack in Iran, oil risk premium to head higher
The U.S. and Iran are careening toward renewed war despite growing hopes this week that the Democrats' decisive midterm election victory will bring the conflict to an end, analysts say.
Crude oil prices fell more than 16% over the last five trading days after U.S. Vice President JD Vance publicly blamed the Republicans' stinging loss on the war. Vance's remarks raised questions about whether the administration still has support to continue the conflict with Iran.
The Democrats plan to use their comfortable majorities in both chambers of Congress to pass a war powers resolution that demands President Donald Trump end the war. But tensions in the Middle East have not eased since the election, and the Democrats aren't sworn in until January, the analysts say.
"Throughout the week, we were struck by the divergence between deepening escalation concerns in the Gulf and the headline-driven off-ramp optimism of market participants thousands of miles away," Helima Croft, head of global commodity strategy at RBC Capital Markets, told investors in a note Friday.
Late Saturday, U.S. Central Command said it disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship after the tanker ignored multiple warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port, according to media reports. Iran state media also reported on explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as several blasts occurring in the port of Jask. CNBC couldn't independently confirm the reports.
Several oil tankers have also come under attack near Oman since the election, killing one seafarer, according to maritime security agencies. Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen continue to fire missiles at neighboring Saudi Arabia.
Meanwhile, the U.S. military buildup continues, with a third carrier strike group en route to the region. The consulting group Rapidan Energy sees an 80% chance that fighting will resume as diplomacy stalls.
Trump told reporters Thursday that he will make a decision soon on whether to attack Iran again.
"I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible but maybe I'll have to," Trump said in the Oval Office. "You'll know soon enough."
"We're locked and loaded," the president said. "If we have to do the rest of the Iran thing, we're very much locked in."
'Very good chance' we go back to conflict in Iran, says fmr. WH senior advisor Amos Hochstein
Crude oil prices will vault above $100 a barrel again in response to renewed fighting, said Bob McNally, president of Rapidan and a former energy advisor to President George W. Bush. Brent crude, the international benchmark, traded above $97 on Friday, while U.S. crude was around $90.
"President Donald Trump is determined as a legacy item, almost at all costs, to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, having them give up their nuclear capabilities," McNally told CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia " on Friday.
"The Iranian regime, on the other hand, is not willing to do it," the analyst said. The escalation dynamic remains in place so long as that core difference between the U.S. and Iran persists, he said.
The risk of war is still alive, especially since Trump no longer faces future elections, said Amos Hochstein, a former energy advisor to President Joe Biden . Gasoline, diesel and jet fuel prices would all surge as a consequence, Hochstein told CNBC's " Power Lunch " Friday.
Tehran has been taunting the Trump administration since the election. The social media account of Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said the "process of the U.S.'s collapse has accelerated" after the midterm results.
And Congress is unlikely to pass a war powers resolution until Democrats take control in January. Trump can veto such a resolution anyway.
The main leverage Congress will have is the power of the purse, Croft said. Government funding expires on Dec. 11, and negotiations for another continuing resolution could drag into 2027, she said. This would give Democrats more leverage when they take power in January, the analyst said.
"Importantly, deferring funding decisions would not immediately constrain Trump's ability to conduct military operations, but could significantly reshape the administration's longer-term funding outlook," Croft told investors.
Trump discussed diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions in the region with the emir of Qatar during a Friday phone call, according to Qatar's state news agency .
An unnamed senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday that Tehran sent a nuclear proposal to the U.S. through Qatar. Tehran will only discuss the proposal after the U.S. meets its demands, the Iranian official told Reuters.
Trump seemed to dismiss the diplomatic efforts Thursday.
"Iran will never have a nuclear weapon," the president said. "They're not doing anything without our approval. It doesn't make any difference what they're looking at," he said of the diplomatic efforts.

QatarEnergy in Talks to Secure Up to 2 mtpa of LNG From NextDecade’s Texas Project | Egypt Oil & Gas
QatarEnergy in Talks to Secure Up to 2 mtpa of LNG From NextDecade’s Texas Project
QatarEnergy is in advanced negotiations with US-based NextDecade to purchase up to 2 million metric tons per annum (mtpa) of liquefied natural gas (LNG) from its Rio Grande LNG export project in Texas, according to two sources familiar with the discussions, Reuters reported.
The potential agreement covers supplies from Train 6 of the project, which remains subject to regulatory approvals and has yet to reach a final investment decision (FID). NextDecade has already committed the full production capacity of the facility’s first five trains through previous sales agreements.
QatarEnergy has been expanding its portfolio of long-term LNG supply agreements with US exporters amid ongoing tensions in the Middle East. The strategy aims to diversify its supply sources and strengthen its trading position against potential disruptions to shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, QatarEnergy CEO Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi told Reuters last month.
In October, QatarEnergy was negotiating purchases of approximately 3 mtpa from each of Venture Global and Woodside Energy. The company has also secured a long-term sales and purchase agreement with Cheniere Energy for 4 mtpa of LNG.
Located near Brownsville, Texas, the Rio Grande LNG project is among the largest LNG export developments in the US. Its first five trains are expected to have a combined production capacity of approximately 30 mtpa once fully operational.
NextDecade submitted a permit application for Train 6 to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) in May and subsequently filed an application with the US Department of Energy in June seeking authorization to export LNG.

NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang Rejects Anthropic’s Total China Chip Ban Push, Says “I Completely Disagree” And Believes “America Is About Competition”
Why would Jensen object when the whole world is fighting for his GPUs?
The geopolitical tug-of-war over AI hardware has sparked fierce disagreement among the Silicon Valley elite. While frontier model creators advocate for total export bans, hardware leaders argue that abandoning global markets undermines American competitiveness. In an interview, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang says he completely disagrees with Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, insisting that American companies must compete rather than retreat.
Jensen Huang fires back at Anthropic CEO over China chip bans, declaring “our market is not his to cede”
During a recent interview with CBS , Huang addressed comments made by Amodei, who urged Washington to completely halt shipments of advanced AI processors and semiconductor manufacturing equipment to China. While Huang agreed that U.S. institutions should receive priority access to domestic technological breakthroughs, he rejected the notion of implementing sweeping trade bans that prevent hardware makers from competing abroad
Related Story NVIDIA’s Development Of Custom HBM Drops Samsung’s And TSMC’s Foundry Rivalry, As Both Manufacturers Join Forces To Develop “Base Die” On The 3nm Node [Update]
“I completely disagree that we should ban China of all American products. The American companies should have advanced capabilities, but then after that, every single layer of the American AI tech stack, including the traditional companies and the AI model companies of every single field and every single chip company, should go and serve the world. Compete for the world, serve the world, capturing market share, capturing economic prosperity. That is all about competing. America is about competition. And we have got to go and compete and not cede entire markets. Our market is not his to cede. Our market is not his to cede. We are to go compete for the world’s market.”
To emphasize America’s existing computational supremacy, Huang revealed that NVIDIA’s next-generation architecture, Vera Rubin , is already shipping in volume production. The cutting-edge platform has been delivered directly to domestic research labs and industry figures like OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Amodei himself, putting the U.S. several years ahead of China. However, Huang cautioned against viewing AI solely through the narrow lens of frontier software models.
“We have to make sure that technology that is created by America advantages America first. Every country would do that, every company does that, every parent does that, every industry does that, every nation does that. And in the case of America, the United States has decided, and I am very supportive, that we provide NVIDIA’s best technology to American companies first. And so we are in the generation of what we call Vera Rubin. Vera Rubin is shipping in volume production. We are several years ahead of China with this technology, and it has been made available to Dario and Sam and the American labs and American industries, and that is exactly what we are doing, and we are delighted to do that.”
NVIDIA’s head honcho described the artificial intelligence ecosystem as a five-layer cake spanning energy generation, raw silicon, foundation models, proprietary data, and end-user applications. While Silicon Valley is heavily obsessed with frontier model developers, Huang stressed that the broader economic revolution happens when legacy enterprises like Walmart and FedEx transform into AI companies. By cutting off international revenue streams, Huang believes that the domestic hardware foundation will weaken.
“On the other hand, remember that AI is a five-layer cake. It is not just that model. The AI industry is represented by the energy sector, the chips sector, the model layer where they are, you could argue that there are six layers or five, but above that is basically the data and the application layer. And we need every single one of these layers, everybody in America, to win. We want us to win in the energy sector, we would like us to lead the world in the chip sector, and we would like to make sure that every single application company wins. I love the fact that FedEx is going to be an AI company. I love the fact that Walmart is going to be an AI company. We need every single company in America to be an AI company, not just one company, not just two companies.”
China currently doesn’t have access to NVIDIA’s B300  GPUs due to the latter being on the U.S. export control list, but a research firm discovered that 32 of these units  were somehow deployed at China Telecom. Whether these GPUs were smuggled or imported through legal means, we cannot confirm, but Jensen Huang’s comments resonate with the global market behavior, and those embroiled in AI will stop at nothing to acquire NVIDIA’s latest and greatest.
Even if the Trump administration sides with Anthropic’s Dario, China has become quite resourceful in bringing overseas hardware and silicon to its shores.

Egypt Eyes Billions in New Investment to Revive Oil and Gas Production
Egypt aims to raise natural gas production to 6.6 billion cubic feet per day by 2027 through increased drilling and foreign investment.
Eni is expanding operations with plans for 230 wells, while its recent offshore gas discovery could accelerate production growth.
Egypt has settled $6.1 billion in overdue payments to energy partners and is modernizing infrastructure to encourage investment.
The Egyptian government is doubling down on its plans to accelerate the development of its oil and gas resources. Egypt now aims to achieve a production capacity of 6.6 billion cubic feet per day by 2027, s upported by increased drilling, new exploration incentives, and greater investment from international oil and gas majors.
In October, the Egyptian Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources, Karim Badawi, met with Cypriot Energy Minister Michael Damianos, East Mediterranean Gas Forum Secretary-General Osama Mobarez and international oil and gas executives from firms operating in Egypt during the “The Future of Energy in Egypt” roundtable to discuss how the country might accelerate investment in the sector and boost production.
The government aims to speed up the development of discoveries and connect them to the country’s existing infrastructure to maximise economic returns from the sector. Badawi said that the ministry hopes to strengthen regional cooperation and establish Egypt as a regional hub. The government plans to address development challenges in partnership with international partners to create the necessary conditions to encourage further investment in the sector.
In recent years, oil and gas production has fallen, largely due to ageing Mediterranean offshore fields, particularly the giant Zohr gas field. The country is seeking greater investment in developing oil and gas discoveries, thereby reducing reliance on mature operations. Egypt hopes to continue using existing infrastructure to reduce the cost of new operations and encourage greater investment in the sector. Egypt is home to vast transportation networks, gas reception, and trading facilities. It has liquefaction capabilities and is strategically located with access to various markets.
During the opening ceremony of the Mediterranean Oil and Gas Conference and Exhibition in October, Badawi said   that Egypt had brought 591 new wells into production and made 113 discoveries between July 2024 and June 2026. The minister said that Egypt had been able to attract higher levels of investment, having successfully paid the outstanding debts that it owed to investment partners in exploration, discovery, and production activities.
Earlier in the year, President Abdel Fattah Al-Sisi announced plans to double crude oil and condensate production as part of a five-year energy strategy during a meeting with Badawi. The government also plans to invest over $4 billion to improve six refineries by modernising existing refineries, raising domestic production of higher-value petroleum products, and reducing Egypt’s fuel import bill.
The five-year strategy focuses on seismic surveys, advanced technologies, new contractual frameworks, and the development of discoveries that have yet to enter production. Al-Sisi has encouraged the government to offer additional incentives to international partners to attract more investment in the sector and encourage new exploration projects.
Al-Sisi also met with the CEO of the Italian oil and gas major Eni, Claudio Descalzi, to discuss expansion. Descalzi stated plans to increase its investment in Egypt, with plans to drill 30 exploration wells and 200 development wells. Eni has invested around $8.5 billion in Egypt to date, producing approximately 242,000 bpd of oil equivalent in 2025 through its subsidiary International Egyptian Oil Company.
Eni aims to increase its production in Egypt by developing new discoveries and leveraging the country’s existing infrastructure to accelerate deployment. Connecting existing infrastructure to new developments will help reduce the time required to advance new projects and extend the operating life of fields already in production. Eni will expand operations in various parts of the country, including the Mediterranean, the Nile Delta, Sinai, and the Western Desert.
The company has already begun using these initiatives and has reported a 50 per cent increase in output from its offshore fields in Sinai. In April, Eni made a significant gas and condensate discovery in the Temsah Concession, located offshore in the Eastern Mediterranean, with preliminary estimates indicating 2 trillion cubic feet of gas and 130 million barrels of associated condensate. The discovery is less than 10 km from existing infrastructure, making it easier to quickly establish connectivity. In August, Eni said that first gas from the discovery would be achieved in less than two years.
In October, Eni announced plans to increase its gas processing capacity in Egypt’s Western Desert through phase two of its Meleiha project in the Merged Meleiha concession. The new facility is expected to process up to 100 million standard cubic feet of gas per day once operational, supporting the government’s aims to accelerate the rollout of new gas production capacity. This will increase the availability of gas for the domestic market, according to the company.
Having settled old debts, Egypt now hopes to encourage greater investment in oil and gas exploration and development over the coming years to help reverse the declining output seen in recent years. Eni has already committed to increasing investment in the North African country and will use Egypt’s existing infrastructure to bring new production online quickly.

Environmentalists criticise choice of Earthshot prize venue owned by fossil fuel firm
Mumbai facility is part of Reliance Industries, owner of world’s biggest oil refinery and funder of controversial mega-zoo
The Prince of Wales’s Earthshot prize will host its forthcoming annual awards ceremony at a venue owned by the billionaire Ambani family conglomerate, drawing criticism from conservationists over their fossil fuel businesses and their foundation’s controversial mega-zoo .
A spokesperson for the Earthshot prize , which awards £1m to five winners every year to invest in conservation work, confirmed to the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay that this year’s ceremony will be held at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on 17 November.
The venue is part of Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, which also owns Jamnagar, the world’s biggest oil refinery in Gujarat on India’s western coast. The group’s philanthropic arm funds the 400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo Vantara, which was founded by Mukesh’s son Anant Ambani and inaugurated by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, last year. The zoo is embroiled in a long-running controversy over its vast collection of more than 150,000 animals, which reportedly includes some of the world’s most endangered species – from the radiated tortoise, native to Madagascar, to the Spix’s macaw, endemic to north-eastern Brazil but now considered extinct in the wild .
Megan Carr, of the Wildlife Animal Protection Forum South Africa (WAPFSA), warned that using a venue owned by Reliance “could lend an unearned environmental prestige to a corporate group currently under question by the global conservation community”.
Conservation groups, including WAPFSA, have raised concerns about the speed with which Vantara has amassed so many animals, and about how they were sourced. The site, near the family’s oil refinery, houses more than 2,000 species of animals.
This week, the 32-member committee that governs Cites, the UN-administered body that regulates trade in endangered species, requested that India submit another report on the steps it is taking to address concerns relating to its imports of protected species.
The committee also requested the Cites secretariat review 11 cases where there are unresolved questions over how animals were sent to Vantara.
Joanna Swift, the executive director of communications at the Earthshot prize, said it had not sought a philanthropic partnership for its award ceremony venue and that it was paying the standard commercial rate to rent the space.
“The [Jio World Convention Centre] was selected because it allowed us to host the event in Mumbai while meeting the practical requirements of an event of this size. It offers world-class facilities, technical infrastructure and experience of hosting major international events, including environmental ones,” Swift said. “In February this year, JWCC hosted the first ever Mumbai climate week.”
Vantara, Kensington Palace and JWCC have been approached for comment.
Vantara has previously denied allegations of wildlife trafficking and says its purpose is “to rescue wild animals in distress, provide treatment along with lifelong care, and rehabilitate those fit for the wild”.
“With regulatory approval, we also breed select endangered or extinct-in-the-wild species, serving as a modern Noah’s Ark to ensure their survival under human care and restore wild populations through reintroduction,” Vantara says on its website.
Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo of allegations that animals had been acquired illegally or mistreated.
A later Cites fact-finding mission raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.
Susan Cheyne, the vice-chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s small apes section, said that Vantara’s model has not yet been shown to support conservation and “may be driving demand for wild animals in trade”.
“For gibbons and other primates, this matters a great deal. Moving animals out of their range countries into a private facility does nothing for wild populations unless there is a transparent, credible plan for those animals: for welfare, for any conservation breeding with clear goals, and for return to range states where that is possible. Real rescue and sanctuary work for primates is done by underfunded centres in range countries,” Cheyne said.
Daniela Freyer, co-founder of the German NGO Pro Wildlife, added: “Our planet is increasingly threatened by the overexploitation of wildlife and by climate change driven by fossil fuels. This week, the Cites Standing Committee, which oversees international wildlife trade, decided to keep India under its compliance procedure, as questions remain about the origin of some of the world’s rarest animals imported to Vantara. A prize whose goals include protecting nature and fixing our climate should be careful not to lend its reputation to these questions.”
Vantara had sought to lobby the UK, the chair of this week’s Cites meetings, attempting to persuade officials to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara, the Guardian and Mongabay reported earlier this month. Ministers were advised not to engage formally with Vantara, internal documents revealed.
The Earthshot prize, founded by Prince William in 2020, is billed as the most prestigious environmental award. William appeared on the BBC’s Graham Norton show last month to promote the prize, saying it was designed to “talk about urgency and optimism together”.
Swift said that it was vital to host an edition of the Earthshot prize in India.
“Mumbai is the sixth largest city on earth. It is home to exceptional environmental solutions and the people behind them, with an impact felt in India and around the world. Spotlighting progress like this, to the largest possible audience, is why the Earthshot prize exists,” Swift said.

items.title: JD Vance gets the Iran war wrong: Diplomacy handed Tehran victory - The Jerusalem Post
items.summary: JD Vance gets the Iran war wrong: Diplomacy handed Tehran victory  The Jerusalem Post
items.content:
Vance blames the Iran war, but diplomacy was the real failure - opinion
The Iran war did not fail because Israel pushed for it. It failed when Washington abandoned its objectives and gave Tehran time to survive.
US Vice President JD Vance speaks at a midterm campaign rally on October 28, 2026 in Kinston, North Carolina.
( photo credit : Tierney L. Cross/Pool via REUTERS )
In a lengthy X/Twitter post after Tuesday's midterm defeat, US Vice President JD Vance laid out why Republicans lost. He cited a pollster who asked Trump 2024 voters who had switched to the Democrats what would bring them back.
According to Vance, four answers accounted for nearly all the responses: end the war, focus on the cost of living, put America first, and change America's relationship with Israel.
Much of the pro- Israel community reacted with outrage at Vance “blaming the Jews.” But on the core diagnosis, Vance is largely right. The war with Iran became deeply unpopular. It drove up gas prices and inflation, and it turned a significant number of Americans against Israel. US President Donald Trump himself called Vance's analysis "largely true." Attacking the messenger accomplishes nothing.
The problem is what Vance wrote next. Referring to the criticism Rachel Campos-Duffy received last Monday for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict with Iran, he concluded that "it turns out her political advice was sound."
That conclusion does not follow. Even if the war cost Republicans Congress, this in no way justifies pursuit of diplomacy with the regime in Tehran. Vance is not merely wrong. He has it exactly backward. The war became a political disaster precisely because the administration abandoned it for diplomacy.
People vote at a polling station at the Buck Creek School, during the US midterm elections on Election Day, in Jefferson County, Kansas, US, November 3, 2026. (credit: REUTERS/Nathan Howard)
On February 28, Trump announced the launch of Operation Epic Fury and laid out four military objectives: destroy Iran's navy, destroy its ballistic missile program, ensure it can never obtain a nuclear weapon, and end its ability to fund and direct its proxies. Reopening the Strait of Hormuz was added a couple of weeks later, after Iran closed it.
Trump did not stop there. The final minutes of that speech were addressed to the Iranian people. He told the IRGC and the police to lay down their arms or "face certain death." He told the Iranian people that "the hour of your freedom is at hand" and urged them, once the bombing was over, to take over their government.
Regime change was not one of the stated military objectives. But it was never really separate from them. A surviving Islamic Republic will rebuild its missiles, its proxy network and its nuclear program the moment it is able to. It was always clear that the only way to achieve Trump's four objectives permanently is to bring down the regime.
For roughly five and a half weeks, the war moved in that direction. American forces concentrated heavily on Iran's navy and missile launch sites. Israel concentrated on the regime itself. The decapitation campaign did not end with the killing of supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on the first day.
It continued for weeks; Ali Larijani was killed about three weeks in. In the final stretch, Israel was striking the IRGC and the Basij, the forces that terrorize and murder Iranian civilians. Israeli drones were hitting their checkpoints and headquarters. Defections had begun. The conditions necessary for the population to return to the streets were underway.
Trump agreed to a ceasefire mediated by Pakistan , whose prime minister had requested a two-week pause to give diplomacy a chance. Trump announced he would suspend the bombing for two weeks. Those two weeks have now stretched to seven months.
What followed was a memorandum of understanding negotiated with Vance in the lead, and Israel cut out of the process. It was one of the weakest diplomatic agreements in recent memory, and it collapsed almost immediately.
The campaign Israel and the US were waging before April 8 never resumed. Later American strikes on Iranian infrastructure were not a return to that war. IRGC and regime leadership have not been attacked since.
None of this should have surprised anyone. Ten days before the war began, I wrote in these pages that Iran was not trying to win a war with the United States. It was trying to survive Trump. The regime knew it could not defeat America militarily.
It also knew Trump had no appetite for a prolonged war. Its strategy was simple: drag the conflict out, keep oil prices high, and let political pressure build in Washington as the midterms approached. For the Islamic Republic, survival is victory. Once Trump is gone, everything the war set out to destroy can be rebuilt.
That is precisely what happened. Every week of negotiations was another week of high gas prices with the regime still standing. Tehran's playbook worked perfectly, and it worked because Washington agreed to play along.
Iran's own behavior shows who it fears. In recent weeks, Tehran has issued statements threatening European governments, Gulf states that host American bases, and American forces directly. The IRGC has warned AI companies that work with Israel. It has even warned Elon Musk over Starlink. Conspicuously, Iran has refrained from threatening Israel.
Since April 8, Iran has fired exactly one missile at Israel and promptly stopped when Israel’s response was too costly. The regime is not afraid of American negotiators. It is afraid of Israel because it knows that Israel is waiting for an opportunity to actually bring down the regime.
Those who wish to argue that Israel pushed Trump into this war may do so. That argument ignores that Trump has been more focused on the Iranian threat than any figure in American public life since the 1980s, but grant it for argument's sake.
Even so, it is incoherent to blame Israel both for starting the war and for how it turned out. The war became a problem because Trump chose the path of diplomacy advocated by Pakistan, Qatar, and Vance himself, against Israel’s wishes.
Diplomacy is not an inherent good. Neville Chamberlain conducted diplomacy too. The question is whether it serves the objective. Seven months of talks with Tehran have produced no deal that holds, no dismantled nuclear program, no end to proxy terrorism, and no freedom for the Iranian people. What they have produced is exactly the outcome that Iran was working towards since April 8.
As politics, Vance's post is shrewd. He kept his distance from the war from the start and was largely absent from public view during the fighting. He reappeared only when the ceasefire talks began. Now he is making sure the defeat does not stick to him. Donald Trump Jr. has already endorsed his analysis.
But shrewd politics is not sound strategy. Trump now faces a choice. According to reports, the options before him are renewed strikes, a deal being drafted by Qatari mediators, or continued blockade and sanctions in the hope that Tehran eventually gives in. Vance and others are pushing for a deal. If Trump takes that road, he will be repeating the very mistake that brought him here.
The voters did not punish the war Israel wanted. They punished the one Washington settled for.
The writer is the executive director of Israel365 Action and co-host of the Shoulder to Shoulder podcast.

items.title: Official Data Shows 450,000 Russians Killed in War, Death Rate Accelerating – Rosstat Leaks - The Moscow Times
items.summary: Official Data Shows 450,000 Russians Killed in War, Death Rate Accelerating – Rosstat Leaks  The Moscow Times
items.content:
A data leak from the Russian state statistics agency Rosstat shows that, according to official figures, over 450,000 Russians have been killed in the war in Ukraine, making the war the fourth most common cause of death in Russia since 2022.
Russia has not officially disclosed its battlefield losses since September 2022 and has dismissed independent estimates as unreliable. Rosstat's figures would make the war in Ukraine Russia's deadliest conflict since World War II, far exceeding the 13,000 Soviet troops killed in the nine-year Soviet-Afghan War.
Rosstat was hit by a cyberattack from Oct.29 and Nov, 1 by the Belarus Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow hacking groups, who posted messages on the organization's homepage. The groups, both banned in Russia as "extremist organizations," stole data on Russia's economy and demographics as well as wartime losses.
"This is the most significant leak of data when it comes to Russian casualties," Janis Kluge, head of the Russia and Eurasia division at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, told The Moscow Times. "I think it's established as a fact that the war has never been more deadly than it is right now."
As well as active servicemen, the figure calculated by the Silent Crow includes civilians killed in airstrikes and Ukraine's 2024 incursion into Russia's Kursk region. The total death toll is likely to be higher as this data does not include soldiers missing in action, nor the 27,000 foreign fighters believed to have been recruited into the Russian armed forces.
The Moscow Times cross-referenced a random sample of 50 names from Mediazona and BBC Russian's " Counting the Dead " open source repository of Russian death records with Silent Crow's leaked dataset, but was unable to verify the data in its entirety.
But the figures are in line with other assessments of Russian casualties; the British Defense Ministry said in early September that over half a million people had died fighting for Russia and casualties could number as high as 1.5 million, including the wounded.
Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, 6.2 Russians have been killed for every kilometer of territory gained. That territory has become increasingly costly each year as the number of registered deaths climbed despite Russia's progress on the front line stalling.
Not all deaths recorded in the database were in combat. 14,160 cases described the death of a member of the Russian armed forces from non-military causes, including illnesses, road accidents or suicide. Over 32,000 died from wounds they had sustained at least a year earlier.
The Belarus Cyber Partisans released a lower figure of 393,881 killed, using a different methodology that only counted the deaths of military personnel or civilians in combat or from the long-term effects of the fighting.
72% of deaths were registered as occurring in the so-called Donetsk People's Republic, where over 20,000 Russian troops were killed in the bloody 10-month Battle of Bakhmut.
The leak supports research showing that Russia's ethnic republics have suffered disproportionately from mobilization and recruitment for the armed forces, with major cities like Moscow registering a smaller share of overall casualties than their populations would suggest.
Researcher Maria Vyushkova told The Moscow Times that the Kremlin's recruitment policies amounted to the "extermination of entire nations" for some of Russia's smallest ethnic groups, attracting men into the armed forces with salaries far more lucrative than anything available locally and generous benefits for their families if they die, or offering a route out of incarceration.
Kluge told The Moscow Times that although Rosstat's figures are dramatic, they may have little economic impact on their own. "This represents around half a percent of Russia's working-age population of 80 million people. That is not enough to make the news because the men who are fighting usually don't have very productive jobs in the first place.
"But the main significance is political," he added. "It's about who is winning this war and you cannot say Russia is winning this war if it is losing population at this rate."

items.title: Ukraine’s new frontier: how space has become critical to balance of the war - The Guardian
items.summary: Ukraine’s new frontier: how space has become critical to balance of the war  The Guardian
items.content:
Ukraine’s new frontier: how space has become critical to balance of the war
In a war driven by drones and battlefield sensors, access to space is essential. After Starlink speed restrictions and Russian Oreshnik missile strikes, Kyiv is racing to develop its own space capabilities
For people in the Russian industrial city of Samara on the banks of the Volga, the first they knew of the Ukrainian attack were detonations that sent a column of smoke into the air.
If the Kremlin was vague about the target, video footage on social media soon made it clear what had been hit in the early hours of 15 August: the Progress Rocket and Space Centre, manufacturer of Russia’s Soyuz-2 rockets.
Two Flamingo missiles had slammed into a pair of buildings, including a facility known as 106A, a “clean room” where motherboards for the Soyuz launch systems were assembled.
Satellite imagery shows damage, including a hole in a roof, at the Soyuz production facility in Samara after Ukrainian strikes in August. Photograph: Vantor In the midst of other Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries and industry, the Samara attack stood out, providing evidence of a spreading war, the geographical impact of which – already felt across Europe via hybrid attacks, and assaults on civilian shipping in the Black Sea – has crept into the domain of space.
In a conflict that is redefining warfare through the heavy use of drones and battlefield sensors, access to space and the satellites that power those systems – as well as the ability to disrupt enemy operations there – has become ever more critical.
The attack on Samara was a case in point, hitting the rockets that deliver Russia’s new Rassvet satellite system, which is being rapidly deployed as a replacement for Elon Musk’s Starlink, from which Russia was shut out earlier this year.
In addition, Ukraine has attacked other sites belonging to Roscosmos this year, including Korolyov, a large complex north of Moscow, and a Ukrainian-built radio telescope captured by Russia in Crimea.
Russia’s attempts to rapidly deploy its Rassvet network are not the only challenge from space that Ukraine faces. Moscow has also used Oreshnik ballistic missiles on at least three occasions – a system that launches into near space, then deploys multiple independently targetable warheads initially designed for nuclear weapons.
All of this has prompted Kyiv to intensify efforts to diversify its own access to space-based systems away from the US and Starlink, which was controversially choked in recent weeks, and to develop new space countermeasures against threats such as the Oreshnik.
Ukraine has conducted at least three tests of near-space interceptions as it has sought to launch its own sovereign satellites, joining a rapidly expanding number of countries working towards a foothold in space.
That became a reality last month when Ukraine and Denmark’s GomSpace announced they had successfully launched the Obria Nano, the first test satellite for a future independent Ukrainian communications network, reportedly envisaging about 245 satellites.
An illustration of the Obria Nano in orbit. Photograph: GomSpace Group AB ‘Everyone wants their own version of Starlink’
The increasing incursion of the Ukraine conflict into space, say experts, is only the latest evidence of the rapid militarisation of a domain the treaties for which remain ill defined, outdated and difficult to enforce.
In September the US air force secretary, Troy Meink, admitted for the first time that Washington had deployed “on-orbit space control weapons” amid reports that Russia had regularly flown its satellites close to US and other countries’ assets in space.
As if to underline that point, a few weeks later a Russian satellite, Kosmos 2612, was observed aggressively manoeuvring towards a commercial radar satellite operated by the Finnish group Iceye that provides three-dimensional terrain imaging to the Ukrainian military, in what experts described as an act of deliberate harassment.
“[Space warfare] has been talked about as the future,” says Dr Elena Grossfeld, an expert on space and security at the Swedish Defence University. “But we’re already in that future.”
For Russia, Grossfeld argues, space has become essential to military success, with Moscow treating offensive operations there as a precursor to broader conflict in a new reality where war is inseparable from satellite-based intelligence and targeting.
“This started before the war in Ukraine,” Grossfield said. “The US Space Force [then second in command, Gen David Thompson] said in 2021 that the US was seeing daily attacks [by Russia and China] on US satellites.
“They are not necessarily kinetic [attacks], but now with the war and with everyone’s dependency on space for intelligence and communications, it has become front and centre.”
While Grossfield said Russia’s intention in the recent “bullying” of the Iceye satellite was not clear, one possibility was to force it to use fuel to change course and in doing so shorten its lifespan.
That is not the only tactic that has been seen. Russia has also used signal jamming, laser-dazzling of satellites, and placed “inspector” spy satellites near foreign space assets.
A Soyuz-2.1b carrier rocket with a military satellite blasts off from the Plesetsk cosmodrome in Russia’s Arkhangelsk region. Photograph: AP Complicating what is happening in space, experts say, is that treaties on governance in space, and deployment of weapons, have in recent years been overtaken.
Victoria Samson, the head of the space security and stability programme at the Secure World Foundation, which advocates for space safety and sustainability, noted a rapid increase in the number of countries operating in space, in tandem with the expansion of commercial activities by companies such as Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin.
But while many countries have opted to use SpaceX for its satellite launches, Musk’s recent actions towards Ukraine, cutting Starlink data speeds, have forced a rapid rethink of whether to rely on unreliable and sometimes ideologically led commercial ventures.
“The big shift in the past decade,” said Samson, “has been towards commercial space operations and that has been an issue in the current conflict [in Ukraine].”
Like Grossfeld, Samson sees frictions in space becoming more overt. “It’s all part of strategic competition,” she said, describing the recent Russian satellite-bullying incident. She added that with more escalation, there had been “more openness on the US side to talk about what they are doing [in relation to weapons in space] while Russia and China are working on a lot of the same stuff.
“Then there is the issue of space being used in an active military conflict. We have already seen Russia jamming GPS, which has resulted in aviation being disrupted over the Baltics. But it has been particularly visible in the issue of Starlink and in pauses by the US to sharing satellite intelligence with Ukraine [that warns] of incoming ballistic missiles.”
If there has been a consequence of Musk’s and the Trump administration’s unreliability, Samson believes, it has been to push countries to seek alternatives. “Like the Russians with [the] Rassvet network, everyone now wants their own versions of Starlink, including the Europeans.”
For Ukraine, said Fedir Venislavskyi, the head of the state security subcommittee of its parliamentary defence committee, that meant a “sovereign” Ukrainian presence in space, now achieved via the Obria Nano satellite.
“Since the war the space domain has been crucial for Ukrainian forces and that has been underlined by recent events – whether at the instigation of the US government or from SpaceX – where we saw communications drop and jeopardise our military’s command-and-control systems.
“Now we need to raise it to another level, not least because the enemy is already threatening Ukrainian territory from international space via Oreshnik missiles. It’s essential we’re not shortsighted about this risk.”
With Russian launch sites now beyond the range of Ukraine’s longest-range missiles, Ukraine has instead conducted three tests on exo-atmospheric kill systems to intercept launches in near space, including launches of weapons piggybacked on very high-flying aircraft.
“It is a priority,” said Venislavskyi. “We’ve already demonstrated launches of exo-atmospheric systems and we are working to see if we can get that in production.” However, he admitted, given the huge demands of the war, funding would be a significant issue.

The S&P 500 Just Had Its Worst Week Since the April 2025 Tariff Crash
SPY slid 3% as AI stocks sank, and NVIDIA alone makes up about 8% of the fund, so your "diversified" index carries heavy chip risk.
Chip stocks plunged 12% and XLK dropped 7%, while the Dow slipped under 1%, showing the pain concentrated in AI hardware.
Hot October jobs data lifted December rate-hike odds to 78%, putting Tuesday's CPI report and NVIDIA's November 17 earnings in focus.
Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)
The S&P 500 closed Friday, November 6, 2026, at 7,376.86, down from 7,580.07 a week earlier. That 2.68% fall was its worst Friday-to-Friday week since the week ending April 4, 2025, when the tariff crash drove a 9.08% correction.
Kevin Frayer / Getty Images The index has now fallen for the fourth straight week. The State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ) lost 2.7%, moving from $755.72 to $735.29.
Most of the damage came on Thursday, November 5. Midterm results set off heavy selling in AI stocks, and the S&P 500 fell 4.36%, its worst day since the April 2025 crash.
The two weeks differ greatly in size. In the April 2025 week, the index fell from 5,580.94 to 5,074.08, a much steeper drop.
The November 6 week set the mark only because the two closest weeks since then just missed it: the week ended May 23, 2025 at -2.61% and the week ended June 5, 2026 at -2.59%.
The losing streak started small. The index fell 1.95%, 0.47% and 0.57% in the weeks ended October 16, 23 and 30. It now sits 5.65% below its October 6 record close of 7,818.93.
Only the S&P 500 can claim the worst-since record. The Nasdaq Composite fell 3.37% for its own fourth straight weekly loss. However, the week ending October 16 was worse for both the Composite, at -4.48%, and the Nasdaq-100, at -5.49%.
