The PHLX Semiconductor Index fell 12.15%, from 10,688.80 to 9,390.25. The Technology Select Sector SPDR ( NYSEARCA:XLK ) fell 7%, and the SPDR energy sector fund fell 11%.
The Dow, which the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:DIA ) tracks, fell just 0.94% to 51,285.73. On Friday, the Dow lost 237.33 points, or 0.46%, while the S&P 500 rose 0.31% and the Composite gained 1.09%. That split shows the losses were concentrated in AI hardware and energy and did not spread across the wider market.
The Invesco QQQ Trust ( NASDAQ:QQQ ) fell 4.98% to $656.10. SPY fell less, but it still carries much of the same risk.
As of SPY's March 2026 fact sheet, NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) by itself made up 7.58% of the fund. The S&P 500 weights each company by its market value, so the AI stocks that pulled the Nasdaq-100 lower also have a large effect on a fund many investors consider "diversified."
All of that AI expansion still has to be powered and cooled by someone, and we featured seven of those suppliers in a free report.
Strong Jobs Data Puts CPI and NVIDIA Earnings in Focus
Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far above the expected 65,000. September's gain was revised to 60,000, and unemployment fell to 4.1%. Traders raised the odds of a December rate hike to 78% from 70%.
Strong hiring can keep wage growth, and with it inflation, running hot, and that gives the Fed a reason to raise rates. Higher rates lower what investors will pay today for profits expected years from now, and highly valued tech stocks depend most on those future profits.
October's consumer price index (CPI), the main inflation report, comes out Tuesday, November 10, at 8:30 a.m. ET. NVIDIA reports fiscal third-quarter results after the close on November 17. A hot inflation number would make a hike more likely, while strong NVIDIA guidance could help steady chip stocks.
What Strategists Are Saying About SPY After the Selloff
Keith Lerner, chief investment officer at Truist Advisory Services, said AI is still the main theme of this bull market and the selloff likely offers a longer-term buying opportunity. Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist at LPL Financial, called the week a knee-jerk reaction to the midterms.
SPY's longer-term trend remains intact. The fund is still up 7.83% for the year, and a slow fall after a run to records looks like an ordinary pullback in a rising market.
Investors exploring ways to reduce AI concentration can compare an equal-weight S&P 500 fund. It gives NVIDIA the same weight as every other company in the index, so swings in chip stocks move it less.
This view would weaken if the S&P 500 closes November 13 below 7,376.86, a fifth straight weekly loss, and NVIDIA's report fails to stop the fall.

items.title: Democrat shaping AI policy bought chip stocks despite backing congressional trading ban - CNBC
items.summary: Democrat shaping AI policy bought chip stocks despite backing congressional trading ban  CNBC
items.content:
Josh Gottheimer discloses AI stock buys after trading ban vote
Rep. Josh Gottheimer disclosed new purchases of AI-linked stocks, including Benchmark Electronics and Applied Materials, as he helps shape Democrats' AI agenda.
The New Jersey Democrat's trades came months after Gottheimer voted to ban lawmakers and their families from buying individual stocks, a restriction he has supported for years.
There's no evidence of wrongdoing, but the investments face fresh scrutiny as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and ramp up oversight of the AI industry.
Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., speaks at a press conference at the Capitol in Washington, Jan. 27, 2023.
Rep. Josh Gottheimer , a Democrat helping write his party's artificial intelligence agenda, has disclosed new purchases of AI-linked stocks — just months after voting to ban lawmakers and their families from buying individual shares.
The New Jersey Democrat disclosed an Oct. 12 purchase of between $1,001 and $15,000 of Benchmark Electronics stock, according to a filing released this week. His jointly owned Morgan Stanley account also bought up to $15,000 worth of Applied Materials shares on Oct. 26, following three earlier purchases of leading AI chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices .
While there's no evidence of wrongdoing, the trades put Gottheimer's investments in the spotlight as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January, gaining new power to regulate and investigate the AI industry.
Gottheimer, a former Microsoft executive, sits on the House Financial Services subcommittee overseeing AI in finance, has introduced legislation on AI regulations and co-chairs a commission developing Democrats' broader AI agenda.
Gottheimer's spokesman, Haraden Bottomley, said the congressman turned over control of his investments to a third party with "full investment discretion" before taking office in 2017.
"Gottheimer is also awaiting approval from Congress of a blind trust. In the meantime, he has taken the extra step of setting up an independent trust," Bottomley said.
Democrats are already targeting the AI industry. Reps. Maxine Waters and Greg Casar introduced a resolution opposing taxpayer bailouts for AI companies, referred in part to Gottheimer's committee. Casar has also called for AI executives to testify under oath, while other Democrats are pushing to restrict data centers or halt new construction altogether.
The purchases also contrast with Gottheimer's longstanding support for restricting congressional stock trading . In July, he was among just 13 Democrats who voted for the Stop Insider Trading Act, which would prohibit lawmakers and their families from purchasing most individual stocks. The bill passed the House but has not become law. Some Democrats opposed it both because it contained a voter-ID provision and because some said it should have gone further in curbing stock purchasing and holding by elected officials.
Four years earlier, Gottheimer backed legislation requiring lawmakers to place investments in blind trusts and pledged to establish one himself.
The AI purchases are just a small slice of Gottheimer's sprawling investment portfolio. The five trades totaled between $5,005 and $75,000, compared with $15.1 million to $59 million in disclosed household assets, including up to $44.5 million in stocks. His household has reported more than 1,100 securities transactions over three years, according to Follow the Filings . Gottheimer reports household assets jointly with his wife, Marla Tusk, who is general counsel at a political consulting firm.
Advanced Micro Devices competes with Nvidia in AI chips, while Applied Materials supplies semiconductor manufacturing equipment. It was also Benchmark's largest disclosed customer in 2025, accounting for 14% of revenue, according to a securities filing .
Benchmark, meanwhile, generated 30% of its third-quarter revenue from semiconductor equipment and another 16% from advanced computing and communications, according to its Oct. 28 earnings report . Gottheimer also disclosed an Applied Materials purchase in August and a sale in September.
The purchases came shortly before a sharp selloff in AI stocks. The Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.5% Thursday, as Nvidia dropped more than 9% and AMD roughly 17%. The index includes both companies.
Benchmark fell nearly 17% over Wednesday and Thursday, closing at $59.34 — roughly 25% below its closing price on Gottheimer's October purchase date — before recovering somewhat Friday.

items.title: Not Nvidia. Not Micron. After the Chip Sell-Off, I'd Buy This AI Stock and Hold It Forever. - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Not Nvidia. Not Micron. After the Chip Sell-Off, I'd Buy This AI Stock and Hold It Forever.  The Motley Fool
items.content:
Semiconductor stocks have dropped over the last month.
Foundry leader Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing already holds a massive market share in the chip manufacturing industry, and it could grow even larger in the years to come.
TSMC trades at a bargain level relative to its potential growth.
Investors have soured on AI stocks. The hyperscalers face pressure as they spend hundreds of billions of dollars annually on their AI build-outs, and several have already dipped into negative free-cash-flow territory. The neoclouds face significant financing challenges as their cost of capital continues to climb. And ultimately, that's all hitting the shares of the semiconductor companies that design and sell the chips that go into the data centers powering the proliferation of AI.
Semiconductor stocks as a class are down by about 30% since Oct. 6 (as measured by the benchmark PHLX Semiconductor Sector index). Few chip stocks have been spared. Nvidia ( NVDA +2.77% ) is down 21%, and Micron ( MU +5.12% ) is down 34%. Smart investors may see this pullback as an opportunity to buy chip stocks at a discount. Indeed, there are a growing number of attractive opportunities in the sector. But I wouldn't buy Nvidia or Micron stock at the current prices.
If I could buy and hold just one AI chip stock right now, it would be Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( TSM +6.33% ) .
The company behind the most advanced chips in the world
Every company that's designing advanced chips for artificial intelligence relies heavily on TSMC to manufacture them. The world's largest third-party foundry has the most advanced chip production processes and the scale to meet the growing demand for advanced chips. As a result, its long-dominant market share has grown to 73% of contract semiconductor manufacturing spend.
TSMC benefits from a virtuous cycle that should ensure it maintains or even expands on that dominance. It generates huge revenues every quarter with a foundry operation that is significantly larger than all of its would-be rivals combined. That provides it with plenty of funds that it can reinvest in research and development to maintain its technological lead. It also provides more capital to invest in expanding its production capacity, enabling it to serve more customers and larger contracts. That, in turn, leads to additional revenue growth, restarting the cycle.
TSMC also benefits from its close working relationships with its largest customers, which help it identify opportunities for performance improvements and plan capital expenditures effectively to avoid overbuilding capacity. While the semiconductor industry is cyclical , TSMC's irreplaceable role in its customers' supply chains helps mitigate earnings volatility. By contrast, Micron and its fellow memory-chip makers continue to face valuation challenges due to the commodity-like nature of the chips they both design and manufacture.

To be sure, TSMC is investing significant capital to expand its production capacity. Management has guided for between $60 billion and $64 billion in capex spending this year, up from $40.9 billion in 2025 and $29.8 billion in 2024. Management expects to continue boosting its capex over the next two years.
But that spending should translate into strong revenue growth.
"The majority of the capex is always related to the long-term demand," CFO Wendell Huang said on the company's third-quarter earnings call. "We have no intention to leave any food on the table for others."
In other words, TSMC is using its dominant position today to ensure it remains the dominant force in contract semiconductor manufacturing for years to come, and to keep delivering strong revenue growth. Management's long-term guidance for 25% compound annualized revenue growth between 2024 and 2029 will need an update after the company grew sales 35.9% in 2025, and that number has accelerated in 2026.
After the recent sell-off in semiconductor stocks, TSMC shares now trade around 21 times forward earnings expectations. That's a similar level to Nvidia, but well above Micron's 4 multiple.
Micron's multiple is significantly lower due to the cyclical and commoditized nature of the memory chip industry . Pricing for memory chips has for decades been much more volatile than logic chips: How much Micron charges for its chips is dictated almost entirely by supply and demand conditions.
Despite a tight supply for the logic chips that TSMC manufactures, it hasn't hiked its prices by an exorbitant amount, and CEO C.C. Wei said TSMC will avoid sudden price hikes. That strategy, combined with its better supply and demand forecasting capabilities due to its position in the market, means TSMC's earnings are much more stable. Micron, by contrast, is expected to see its earnings start to drop in 2029 as more memory-chip manufacturing capacity comes online across the space and supply starts to catch up with demand.
While Nvidia is growing significantly faster than TSMC with much lower capital intensity, TSMC is the better long-term investment at the current price. It stands to benefit from the growing demand for semiconductors regardless of which companies are designing tomorrow's most popular data center chips. Its leading position in the industry is unlikely to change anytime soon. In other words, it's more predictable than Nvidia, which makes it a more attractive long-term opportunity.
With expectations for revenue growth well above 20% and TSMC's ability to maintain wide operating margins, the stock at its current earnings multiple looks like a bargain.

items.title: Mapping how France’s protest wave spread across Europe
items.summary: More than 1,700 cost-of-living demonstrations have hit 31 European countries since mid-September, led by France.
items.content:
Share Mapping how France’s protest wave spread across Europe on social media
France’s protest movement is showing little sign of easing, nearly two months after high school students first walked out over crumbling classrooms.
On Saturday , 146,000 people rallied across the country, including 46,000 in Paris, according to the Ministry of the Interior, while unions put the figures at 250,000 and 75,000.
Turnout was down from previous weeks, but police used tear gas and batons on protesters in Paris and fired tear gas canisters at hundreds of people blocking a road in central Lyon, France’s third-largest city. About 70,000 security personnel were deployed, days after an estimated 575,000 people joined a union-organised rally.
The protests have expanded to cover a range of issues, from high fuel prices to wages and social housing, and in some cases, the demonstrations have been marred by looting and violence. Police have been accused of using excessive force, with officers using barricades, tear gas and batons against protesters.
Al Jazeera maps where demonstrations, including riots, have taken place across Europe.
An analysis of data from Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) found that between September 15 and October 30, more than 1,200 protests and riots of 100 or more people took place across France over education, public services and the cost of living.
The movement began in mid-September in high schools, where students complained of overcrowded classrooms, a lack of teachers and crumbling buildings. It soon broadened into protests against the rising cost of living, drawing in trade unions and the “yellow vests” movement, with rioting and looting on the sidelines.
On October 17 alone, more than 500,000 people protested nationwide, according to government estimates.
A vandalised car near the Marianne statue at the Place de la Republique, with a yellow vest placed on it, the day after clashes during nationwide demonstrations against the cost-of-living crisis and rising fuel prices, in Paris, France, October 18, 2026 [Abdul Saboor/Reuters] ACLED CEO Clionadh Raleigh said on October 19 that ACLED had recorded an average of 20.5 demonstrations a day in France over the past five years. “During the current protest cycle, that has jumped to almost 66 a day, more than three times the usual rate,” she said.
Protest cycles typically last about 20 days, or 36 for major movements, Raleigh said. By ACLED’s count, this one had reached 45 days and was still going.
“But the most striking difference is the level of confrontation,” she said. “Almost a quarter of events, 24.2 percent, have been classified as riots, compared to a median of just 1.9 percent in previous cycles. Only the unrest following the death of Nahel Merzouk in 2023 recorded a higher proportion.”
The police response has also drawn criticism. On October 28, four United Nations experts mandated by the Human Rights Council expressed alarm at the “excessive use of force” by French authorities in dispersing the student protests.
A police officer throws a tear gas canister at a protester during a demonstration against rising living costs in Rennes, France, October 24, 2026 [Jeremias Gonzalez/AP Photo] “The scale of the arrests and detention, affecting several thousand people, mainly minors, appears disproportionate and deters demonstrators from exercising their freedoms of expression and peaceful assembly,” they said in a statement .
In the northern city of Lille, a teenager lost a hand when a grenade exploded as school protesters clashed with police.
France is not protesting alone. Since mid-September, demonstrations over rising living costs, low wages and a lack of public services have broken out in 30 other European countries, from Portugal to Poland.
Between September 15 and October 30, more than 1,700 protests and riots of 100 or more people took place across Europe, according to an analysis of ACLED data.
Although protests in other countries did not reach the same scale as the rallies in France, they may be a sign of discontent spilling over, Alberto Alemanno, professor of European Union law and policy at HEC Paris Business School, told Al Jazeera last month.
“France is the epicentre of this movement … and there are signs now that this is spreading beyond France,” Alemanno said.
France has led the demonstrations, but protests have also broken out across Europe at the same time, driven by a common thread of underfunded education, rising living costs and unaffordable housing.
According to an analysis of ACLED data, France saw more than 1,200 protests and riots between September 15 and October 30, followed by Spain (173), Italy (160), Germany (70) and Portugal (33).
Demonstrators clash with police during an antigovernment protest organised by the Italia in Piazza movement, in Milan, October 17, 2026. Inspired by protests in France and Spain, demonstrators protested against the rising cost of living, low wages, high rents and public service shortcomings, demanding better living and working conditions [Piero Cruciatti/AFP] In Spain, tens of thousands of people rallied in early October after parliament rejected two emergency housing decrees on October 2, dealing a blow to Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s minority government.
In Italy, demonstrations over the cost-of-living crisis and unaffordable housing have led to clashes with police.
In Portugal, tens of thousands of protesters marched against the cost-of-living crisis, low wages and an inability to access housing in major cities.

Beijing’s latest property stimulus package has failed to stop a downward spiral in home transactions and prices in mainland China’s lower-tier cities, which could prompt top regulators to roll out stronger incentives to reinvigorate the weak market.

items.content:
About 600,000 of Nvidia's artificial intelligence (AI) chips are reportedly piled up in Hong Kong, unable to enter mainland China. The U.S. government allowed exports, but China has not approved large-scale imports.
China's big tech companies need high-performance U.S. chips to develop AI models, but the Chinese government is wary of rising dependence on U.S. technology. Policies aimed at protecting the domestic chip industry are instead becoming an obstacle for Chinese AI companies to secure chips.
On the 5th (local time), Reuters, citing two sources familiar with the matter, reported that about 600,000 of Nvidia's high-performance AI Semiconductor H200 chips are being stored in Hong Kong, unable to be brought into mainland China. This is the first time the specific quantity of H200s stacked in Hong Kong has been reported.
The Chinese government has in recent months allowed the entry of some H200s. Several major Chinese internet companies are each said to have secured about 10,000 H200s. Small quantities have also come in through brokers or indirect channels. However, authorities are still not approving large-scale imports.
◇ Need U.S. chips, but protecting domestic industry comes first
This situation stems from the overlap of U.S. export controls and China's chip self-sufficiency policy. Since 2022, the United States has restricted China's access to advanced AI Semiconductors and chipmaking equipment. The move aimed to keep China's advanced technology development in check. The H200 had been subject to the U.S. export ban, but the Donald Trump administration changed policy after last year's U.S.-China trade talks to allow sales to approved Chinese customers.
Separately, the Chinese government is maintaining its own import restrictions. If large volumes of U.S. chips flow in, domestic companies may keep choosing Nvidia products, which outperform Chinese-made offerings. That could clash with policy goals for Chinese chipmakers to expand their market and build technological capabilities.
It is in the same vein that China is not completely blocking U.S. chips. In AI model training, which is hard to replace immediately with Chinese products, U.S. chips are allowed on a limited basis, while in deploying AI models in actual services, the aim is to increase the use of Chinese chips.
Earlier, the information technology (IT) outlet The Information reported in July that authorities had notified Alibaba, ByteDance Ltd., and DeepSeek that they could allow limited purchases of H200s for AI model training. The Information said total approved volume could come in under 200,000 units. China is said to have required that domestic chips be used first for "inference," which deploys AI models in actual services.
AI model training is the process of processing vast amounts of data to improve a model's performance. Inference is the task of using a trained model to answer questions or generate outputs. The view is that by distinguishing training from inference to manage chip use, the Chinese government aims to secure the performance needed for AI development while growing the domestic chip market.
Semiconductor chips placed on a printed circuit board. The photo is unrelated to the article. /Courtesy of Reuters
◇ The paradox of technological self-reliance: burden in securing high-performance chips
The problem is that Chinese chips still do not fully match the performance of Nvidia's products. The H200 is not Nvidia's latest AI Semiconductor, but it is evaluated as offering performance that Chinese substitutes have not caught up to. It is especially useful for training large-scale AI models when combined with Nvidia's software.
As major Chinese tech companies such as Alibaba, ByteDance Ltd., and Tencent expand AI services, demand is also rising for high-performance chips like the H200. The drive by China's big tech firms to secure other U.S.-made chips is related to this demand.
Reuters reported last month that ByteDance Ltd., Alibaba, and Tencent ordered more than 3 million of Nvidia's RTX Pro 5500 graphics cards. The product is less powerful than the H200 but complies with U.S. export rules, and the list prices for the order volume total more than $35 billion (about 47 trillion won).
◇ Server asking prices surge in the gray market amid import limits
In particular, as U.S. export controls and China's import limits intersect, prices are surging in the unofficial chip market. According to Reuters, at the end of Oct., a server equipped with eight H200 chips in mainland China was offered for sale at more than 6 million yuan (about 1.2 billion won). That is about triple the price a year earlier. Servers equipped with Nvidia's next-generation Blackwell chips, which are subject to U.S. export controls, were reportedly offered at more than 20 million yuan (about 4 billion won) per unit.
Analysts say China's chip self-reliance policy could raise development costs for domestic AI companies in the short term. If imports are restricted when Chinese chips cannot fully replace Nvidia's products, securing high-performance chips could become even harder. Depending on whether the government approves large-scale imports in the future, Chinese AI companies' chip supply and development costs are also expected to be affected.

items.title: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, Barnier tells BBC
items.summary: The former Brexit negotiator says EU countries would reject any British attempts to follow economic rules "a la carte".
items.content:
Figure caption, Michel Barnier says there will be 'no cherry-picking' in a deal for the UK to returns to the EU
The EU's former Brexit negotiator has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes, after Andy Burnham said he wanted to explore closer economic ties with Europe.
The prime minister has said rejoining the bloc's internal market was among options he could pursue as part of a reshaping of ties since the UK's exit from the EU nearly six years ago.
But Michel Barnier told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that EU members would insist on the UK readopting certain conditions, such as the free movement of people, to gain access.
He said there was not a "single market Ã  la carte" menu from which the UK could pick and choose what elements it wanted to adopt.
Barnier - who led the EU delegation during Brexit talks between 2016 and 2021, and had a three-month spell as French prime minister in 2024 - said the "door is open" within Europe to the UK rejoining as an EU member.
But he insisted that any move to rejoin the single market - which allows for goods to be freely traded without border controls - would require the UK to follow the same terms as other members.
He added that this included compliance with regulations designed to promote the circulation of goods, services, capital and people, referred to collectively within EU institutions as the "four freedoms".
"There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market."
Since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham has suggested he could commit Labour to pursuing a much closer future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member, though he has ruled out major changes before the next election.
His predecessors have struck a series of deals with the EU on different aspects of how the UK and EU interact post-Brexit.
Both sides are hoping to use a meeting in Brussels in 10 days' time to unveil deals on food standards, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime .
Why the prime minister wants to talk about Brexit again
Of the four freedoms, the free movement of people - which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa - was a key issue during the 2016 Brexit referendum.
Burnham's immediate predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, ruled out re-establishing it for the UK in Labour's 2024 election manifesto and any move to advocate it again would prove a key dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK at a future poll.
Burnham recently said in an interview that he would not re-establish free movement of people without a referendum, prompting Downing Street to clarify that he was not advocating its return at this point.
He has previously said he wanted to lay out "different options" for the relationship with Europe at the Brussels summit later this month, before trying to find a consensus with the British public on a new relationship.
Barnier also predicted that EU countries would reject reinstating the British financial rebate, first negotiated in 1985, that lowered UK contributions towards the EU's annual budget while it was a member.
The UK's decision to leave the bloc had created "a new situation", he said, meaning a new rebate would be "off the table".
Barnier also compared Reform leader Nigel Farage to French politician Marine Le Pen. He said: "We have our own Farage. It is Mrs Le Pen. The same populism, the same lies, the same false promises."
Asked by Kuenssberg to clarify what he was referring to with his accusation of lies, Barnier said "for instance, when Mr Farage and Mr Johnson promised the UK people to get back [Â£350] million per week, it was not true, it was not possible. It was a lie".
The Vote Leave campaign, of which Boris Johnson became a key figure, has been criticised previously for the slogan on the side of their campaign bus that said Britain sent Â£350m a week to the EU, adding: "Let's fund our NHS instead".
Johnson said in 2017 that "once we have settled our accounts, we will take back control of roughly Â£350m per week. It would be a fine thing as many of us have pointed out if a lot of that money went on the NHS".
Critics have said that the Â£350m per week was an approximate sum which represents a "gross contribution" and did not take into account the UK's Â£75m-a-week rebate nor the EU's investments in the UK.
Johnson has since defended the claim, saying the Â£350m was based on the UK's gross contribution to the EU, and was in fact an underestimate as UK contributions were due to rise.
âIn his memoirs published in 2024, Johnson said EU money spent in the UK was not "democratically controlled by the British people", and "even if the net figure was only Â£175m, that was still a hell of a lot of money".
Farage, who led Leave UK and was not part of the Vote Leave campaign so not connected to the Â£350m claim, said: "It is the same old Barnier - arrogant, out of touch and a bully. He vindicates our decision to leave every time he opens his mouth."

items.title: The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
items.summary: Republicans can stick with Trumpism or chart a new path, writes BBC Washington correspondent Daniel Bush.
items.content:
By Daniel Bush ,Â  Washington correspondent Â  and Â  Madeline Halpert
Republicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.
The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.
But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.
The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".
Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy.
"There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.
The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away.
It's too early to tell which faction will win. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.
The party must decide whether it will be "centred on one figure, one guy, or on a wider set of ideas like conservatism that can win outside the deepest red places," Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.
Critics on the right - the "Never Trumpers" who opposed his first White House campaign - are pushing for a return to the Republican Party's pre-Trump roots, citing the historic losses around the country on election night.
But simply turning back the clock on Trump will be extremely difficult if not impossible to do.
The party has been wholly transformed during Trump's decade-long reign. Most Republicans have shifted to the right on domestic issues like immigration, and rejected the interventionist foreign policy of the George W Bush era that led to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.
In Congress, the more moderate establishment wing of the party that disliked Trump from the start has almost entirely disappeared, replaced by conservative Trump backers who echo his nativism and populist rhetoric.
That trend continued this year, as old-guard Republicans like John Cornyn in Texas and Maine's Susan Collins, both of whom clashed with Trump over the years, were voted out of office.
Three days after the election Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff , replacing Susie Wiles.
The move signalled Trump has no plans to moderate his policies or message in his remaining years in office. Miller, who had been serving as the president's chief domestic policy adviser, is a longtime Trump aide known for his hardline immigration policies.
With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle
One of the architects of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, Steve Bannon, predicted a "civil war" in the party after the midterms.
Afterwards, he blamed the Republicans' defeat on the economy and "foreign wars". "I don't think we implemented the Maga programme," he said, calling on Trump to double down on mass deportations.
But other Republican strategists said the midterms were a wake up call for Make America Great Again (Maga) loyalists who want Trump's political movement to outlast his presidency.
"There's still plenty of Maga voters out there who have supported Donald Trump through thick and thin," said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist.
"But there is also a significant portion of the Republican Party that's non-Maga, and that's a majority now."
Should Republican hopefuls distance themselves from Trump?
The party lost control of the House and Senate, as well as governorships and state legislatures in red states like Texas and Kansas where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades - and where Trump won by double digits when he was on the ballot.
The stunning upsets underscored the fickle nature of political coalitions.
Trump expanded the Republican base in 2024, increasing support with Latinos and younger voters among other key groups. Republicans hailed the gains as a sign of future strength for the party.
Just two years later, the party lost ground with nearly every critical voting bloc. According to a New York Times analysis of voter data, Latino support for Democratic candidates increased by 29 percentage points from 2024-26. Support from young voters 18-29 years old increased by 33 points.
The swings reflected polling ahead of the midterms that found widespread disapproval with Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and the war with Iran.
Image caption, Tuesday night saw Trump's Republicans lose in states they had comfortably held for decades
Democrats also capitalised on a public perception that the Trump family and administration is rife with self-dealing and corruption. The president's focus on the White House ballroom and other Washington construction projects also contributed to a sense among voters that he was more focused on his legacy than addressing affordability issues.
It's a sentiment shared by Benjamin Shrader, the leader of the Young Republicans in Austin, who was still shell-shocked when he spoke to the BBC in Texas the morning after his party was almost wiped out in the state by a Democratic "blue tsunami".
Shrader said Trump was still a "force of nature" when asked to reflect on how the president had used his first public appearance after the results to show off the White House ballroom project.
He hesitated before adding: "I would focus on issues that are not ballrooms, that are not renaming things. I would focus on what matters."
The evidence in the immediate aftermath of the midterms suggests that Republicans could benefit by distancing themselves from Trump ahead of 2028.
Figure caption, With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?
'Vance was the favourite - now the race is wide open'
Vance tried to thread the needle with his midterm assessment blaming the Iran war and calling for a return to "America First." It was a nuanced critique that broke with Trump on an unpopular war, but embraced a broader political brand that remains popular with the Maga base.
Trump's next moves on Iran will be watched closely by the party for their 2028 implications. An escalation would risk fuelling the concerns voiced by Vance and other "America First" proponents.
In his postmortem statement on X, Vance also echoed the growing calls on the right to reexamine US support for Israel. But he also signalled an openness to making some immigration enforcement changes. That clashes with Miller, a Vance ally who has speared the administration's second-term immigration agenda.
Party strategists said the midterm drubbing complicated Vance's path to the nomination.
"Before this midterm, JD Vance was the odds-on favourite to win the Republican nomination in 2028. After this midterm, the nomination battle is completely wide open," Ayres said.
Potential Trump successors have some time to consider their options, but they'll have to make up their minds relatively soon. Any 2028 presidential hopefuls will face pressure to announce White House bids in the next few months. Some could launch campaigns before the end of the year.
Vance's election analysis was widely interpreted as an unofficial signal of his plans to run. It will likely be a crowded primary field.
Image caption, Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are seen as contenders for the 2028 nomination
Other rumoured White House contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Governor DeSantis, former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, to name a few.
In the next election cycle, Republican presidential and congressional candidates alike will have tough decisions to make on key issues of the day, from US support for Israel to tariffs to the AI boom.
Trump's power may be diminished as he enters the final two years of his second term, but he'll still have the loudest voice in the party over the next two years. It's unclear whether he will get deeply involved in the process or take a hands-off approach.
Trump has praised Vance and Rubio at different times, but typically deflects questions about who he'd like to see succeed him.
His endorsement will loom as the biggest wildcard in the 2028 Republican primary race.
"It remains to be seen who will jump into that race," Ayres said.
"But I think it's going to be a lot larger and more diverse than we anticipated before the midterm election."
Figure caption, 'Hopefully things get done': Americans react to historic political shift

If the Fed Raises Interest Rates in December, I'm Making This 1 Investing Move
The Federal Open Market Committee decided not to raise interest rates when it last met on Oct. 28, but a rate hike in December is expected.
In the Federal Open Market Committee's (FOMC) last summary of projections, members targeted a year-end median federal funds rate of 4.1%. The rate is currently in the 3.75% to 4% range, so their median projections would suggest one more rate hike this year.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Does that mean the Federal Reserve will raise rates when it meets next on Dec. 8-9? No, but based on the fact that inflation keeps rising and the FOMC itself said it was likely, it is widely anticipated.
At the time of this writing, the CME FedWatch survey says that 68% of interest rate traders expect a rate hike in December, while 32% say that rates will hold. No one sees rates declining in December.
As for the longer-term projections, the dotplot indicates that rates will be at 4.1% in 2027, which means they see no movement next year, assuming a rate hike in December. The CME FedWatch poll says 34% expect rates at 4.25% to 4.50% a year from now, in December 2027. That would indicate two rate hikes from the current range.
Some 33% say rates will be at 4% to 4.25% next year, while 11% say they will be where they are now, 3.75% to 4%. Only 1% anticipate rates declining in 2027 to the 3.50% to 3.75% range.
While these projections are subject to change, investors should anticipate that rates will rise in December and stay high at least through 2027 -- and likely beyond. Should that alter your investment strategy?
As a long-term investor, the fluctuating interest rate should not, in itself, signal that any major portfolio moves need to be made.
That seems particularly true in this case. This does not appear to be the beginning of a Fed tightening regime like we saw in 2022. In 2022, inflation was rising rapidly and rates had been at 0%, so it was clear that rates would be moving steadily higher for quite a while to cool down inflation.
This is a very different environment. Rates had already started to come down as inflation had been under control, but tariffs followed by the war in Iran and its impact on energy prices has begun to move inflation higher.
But the Fed has given no indication in its dotplot or statements that this is the start of an aggressive plan to hike rates. It is more likely that rates will hover around where they are now, maybe moving slightly higher, but staying roughly where they are, at least in 2027. It's what many call a higher-for-longer scenario.
Of course, things can change ... just like they did last year. In December 2025, rates were lowered to 3.50% to 3.75% and the expectation was for one rate cut in 2026 to 3.25% to 3.50%, and one more rate cut in 2027 to 3% to 3.25%. But, the war in Iran happened and instead of a rate cut, we got a rate hike.
With the Democrats winning the House and Senate on Nov. 3, there is strong sentiment to end the war, eliminate the Trump tariff increases, and rebuild trade relationships. This could potentially bring down prices and lead to rate cuts instead of rate hikes. And it may not -- but the point is, these projections are not set in stone and could certainly change.
That's why, as an investor, the first thing I would do if the FOMC raises rates in December is to sit tight and do nothing.
This doesn't appear to be the start of aggressive rate tightening, and it is likely that rates will hold steady for a while. There is even a chance that they start to move back down next year.
Even before the election, the FOMC, in its September dotplot, expected inflation to be down to 2.3% at the end of 2027, so there is an expectation for declining inflation -- and that would be a good thing for rates.
But in the broader view, even if rates dipped in 2027, it will probably not be a major shift. You should be prepared for a stable, but higher-for-longer rate environment.
At the end of 2027, after the FOMC acts, investors should review their portfolios as a matter of course. This is especially true with a new Congress coming in and new policies. There could certainly be some changes afoot that impact your portfolio at the margins, but right now it's too early to tell.
Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.
But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.
While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

items.title: 'Flat', 'tired', 'cynical': Unusually gloomy Kiwis deliver New Zealand's tightest election in years
items.summary: The national mood is low, and faith in politics even lower - with voters deserting the major parties at the polls.
items.content:
Figure caption, New Zealand election 'too close to call' - so who's won?
New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather.
"It's pretty flat," 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger says. "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread."
"Tired. I think we're all tired," Symone, 28, admits.
"I didn't even vote," one man in his 40s sheepishly confesses. He couldn't bring himself to tick any of the boxes, he explains, declining to chat further.
"Wellington's a bit of a bubble," another voter says, expressing a caveat I heard often, before describing feeling disillusioned.
But polling shows this is a pervasive sentiment across the country: the national mood is low and faith in politics is even lower.
More than half the country no longer sees it as a land of opportunity, a recent study found, while a similar portion fears that the future looks even worse.
Many Kiwis feel the economy is in ruins, there are no jobs, the cost of living has become sky high, the sense of community that used to be a source of national pride is breaking down and there's no sense of genuine progress on policy solutions.
A record number of them are abandoning ship in search of brighter futures elsewhere.
Saturday's election also saw a record number of voters desert the two major parties, giving neither a clear mandate.
But it brought new highs for parties across the spectrum: the left-leaning Greens, the right-wing libertarian Act Party and the centrist Opportunity Party â the latter of which had never won a seat in parliament before but could now hold the balance of power with seven.
Image caption, The Opportunity Party says it is willing to work with either of the major parties
"You have voted to change New Zealand politics for good," the party's ecstatic leader Quilae Wong told Kiwis on election night. "I personally came into this because I was frustrated at the slow pace of change."
It will likely be weeks before we know exactly who will make up the governing coalition and what deals have been made to form it.
But this is only the first of many challenges facing whoever is the next prime minister of a country at a crossroads.
For a long time, the country was viewed as a land of milk and honey â literally â for those who worked hard, with its people ranking amongst the most positive in the world.
A satisfying career, access to quality healthcare, and a close network of family and friends â which research suggests are the three most important building blocks of a happy life â were all there for the taking, University of Auckland Prof Robert MacCulloch says.
"The lifestyle was good," the world-leader in the study of happiness economics tells the BBC. "You weren't the highest paid, but you could get by nicely."
Image caption, Many young people like Michael Dawson (left) feel like they can't get ahead
Many who spoke to the BBC said the country's decline accelerated into a dive during the Covid pandemic.
Unemployment is now at an 11-year high and rising. For Kiwis aged under 24, things haven't been this bad in three decades: jobs are so scarce that one in three either cannot get enough work or have none at all.
Michael Dawson says he did everything he thought he was supposed to: finished school, studied a trade and obtained a qualification, and has applied for dozens of jobs.
But it's been a year now and the job market is so dire he hasn't had a single interview.
"It has sucked. A lot... I'm somewhat cynical with the way I think [about the future] now," the 20-year-old says.
Zainab Ali, chief executive of support service Youth Inspire, has never seen demand so high, with waitlists for its employment aid workshops stretching into the hundreds.
The young people who do make it through their doors on the outskirts of Wellington are disheartened.
"The things we used to hear from everyone's grumpy uncle around the Christmas table sometimes, our young people are now starting to give us that same feedback: like, 'What's the point?'"
Image caption, Sam says he's flirted with a move to Australia
Meanwhile, household electricity bills have jumped drastically, partly driven by global supply shocks. New Zealand remains one of the least affordable places on Earth to rent or buy a home. High inflation means every dollar is having to stretch further.
The island nation produces enough food to feed its population eight times over, but about a quarter of adults are skipping meals because the price of groceries â set by a supermarket duopoly â is among the highest in the developed world.
And the headlines are full of healthcare crises: long waiting lists, chronic understaffing, crumbling health infrastructure and climbing costs for patients. Few stories have captured the state of the system like the death of a man who collapsed in an emergency department toilet after a nine-hour wait in July.
"There's a segment of the population that are facing real material hardship... and then there's another segment of New Zealanders that are quite anxious that they could be next," political scientist Luke Oldfield, from Victoria University of Wellington, says.
Increasingly polarised public debate â around topics like MÄori rights and the Treaty of Waitangi, healthcare for LGBT+ people and immigration â have added to the mental load for many in those communities.
"There's been a few groups feeling like they're being used as a political football," Dr Lara Greaves, who studies Indigenous politics, says.
This perfect storm is driving about 180 people to leave the country every day â a record-breaking exodus that is dividing families, shrinking communities and draining talent pools.
Siblings Sam and Emily tell the BBC that they love New Zealand but find it hard to keep finding reasons to stay. Their friends are leaving en masse and even their parents have considered moving to Australia.
"It's not just that you're being rewarded for going to Australia, it's that you're kind of actively being punished for staying here," Sam says.
Image caption, Stu thinks New Zealand is on its way back up
There are still large parts of the country that feel differently, though.
At the nation's largest livestock saleyard in the town of Feilding, where farmers from all over the island have gathered, Stu Morton says the last year was the best he's had in his 30-year career.
The agriculture industry - which makes up about 3% of New Zealand's GDP - was struggling under the previous Labour government's emissions reductions scheme, he adds, but has turned a corner under the National Party.
He believes the rest of the economy will follow suit.
"We've been through those times where you're questioning 'Where's the future?'
"What helps is having a stable government... [and] it comes down to a positive attitude - appreciating that what you've got is actually okay."
Many of these issues affecting New Zealand are global trends - and it's undeniable that Kiwis' standard of living is better than many others.
But these issues are having a corrosive impact on its national identity.
"It leads to a crisis of confidence about what New Zealand is and where it's going," Helen Clark, who was prime minister from 1999 to 2008, tells the BBC.
Her foundation surveys New Zealanders every year about social cohesion, and its most recent report found Kiwis - in particular young people - feel far more isolated than they did a generation ago, attitudes towards multiculturalism are souring and the population is becoming less hopeful.
Faith in institutions and leaders has taken an alarming turn: only two out of five New Zealanders trust the government to do the right thing, while less than half of the country trusts the courts.
"There's a feeling that, really, there's no-one who cares," Clark says.
Image caption, National Party leader Christopher Luxon is seeking a second term
The transformation former Labour prime minister Jacinda Ardern promised on issues like healthcare and housing when she was elected in 2017 never eventuated. Many other achievements - for example world leading smoking reforms, emissions reduction policies or MÄori language initiatives - have been wound back by her successors.
Her legacy is dominated by polarising Covid decisions, as is Chris Hipkins', who was health minister before his eight months in the top job after Ardern's resignation .
The National Party came to power in 2023 promising to "get our country back on track" and rebuild the economy.
"You'd have to say they've had very limited success," political commentator Grant Duncan says. "And the Luxon government can only blame the previous government for so long."
National delivered the education overhaul it pledged, but the biggest moment of their tenure was the massive hikoi â protest march â led by MÄori over their coalition partner's unpopular bill to redefine the Treaty of Waitangi. And then came the two leadership challenges Christopher Luxon fought off in the past six months.
Image caption, Former PM Chris Hipkins has been leader of New Zealand's centre-left Labour Party since January 2023
There's a sense Labour had too much ambition, much of it costly and unfulfilled, while National doesn't have enough, having spent much of its time and effort wrangling their own flank.
Both governments say their plans for the country were stymied by crises out of their control â such as Covid, the Iran war and US trade antagonism.
But Duncan says that's not cutting it with voters. He's never seen the country quite like this before: "Neither of the parties has been able to field a really strong, inspiring leader. Both of them have a track record of disappointing results."
No matter who ends up taking the top job, Sam says he's not convinced much will change.
"It does just feel stale... a lot of the population probably feels like we could do a bit better," he says. With a wry smile, he adds: "I don't think it helps that they're two white guys named Chris."

Saturday November 7, 2026 12:50 pm PST by Mitchel Broussard
Black Friday is now just a few weeks away, taking place on Friday, November 27 in 2026. As always, this will be the best time of the year to shop for great deals, including popular Apple products like AirPods, iPad, Apple Watch, and more.
Note: MacRumors is an affiliate partner with some of these vendors. When you click a link and make a purchase, we may receive a small payment, which helps us keep the site running.
Specifically, in this article we're sharing all of the Apple products that currently have all-time low prices, or discounts that are at least close to their record-low prices. Of course, these are early Black Friday deals, so even better discounts could emerge later in the month, but if you're shopping right now these are all the best prices around.
You can use the links below to jump directly to the section you're shopping for today.
Apple Watch Ultra 3 (Milanese Loop) for $649.00 ($250 off)
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 has dropped to $699.99 on Amazon in one of the most notable early Black Friday discounts, down from $799.00. This is a match of the all-time low price on the new Ultra 4, which just launched in September.

iPhone Duo : Up to $1,200 off with eligible trade-in
Apple Watch SE 3: No cost (up to $300) when adding a watch line on a qualifying plan, or get $250 off any Apple Watch when picking up another Apple Watch

Additionally, new and existing customers can get up to $1,200 off the iPhone Duo with an eligible trade-in. If you're switching to AT&T, the carrier will give you up to $800 to pay off your current device balance, and you can save $200 per line when ordering the smartphone online.

items.title: As war rages in their home country, Ukrainians find shelter, community in an Elkhorn apartment complex - Nebraska Public Media
items.summary: As war rages in their home country, Ukrainians find shelter, community in an Elkhorn apartment complex&nbsp
items.content:
As war rages in their home country, Ukrainians find shelter, community in an Elkhorn apartment complex
Karolina Ohnivchuk, left, with Oleksandr and Varvara Babishkevych, learn English together at Elk Hills Apartments in the Elkhorn area. The trio are reading the children’s book “Because of Winn-Dixie” to help with their English. (Photo by Lily Smith/Flatwater Free Press)
Karolina Ohnivchuk’s fingers traced the words on the page, brow furrowed in concentration.
She listened as her neighbors, Oleksandr and Varvara Babishkevych, slowly recited English sentences from well-loved paperbacks. Paging through the children’s book, they read of the dog who couldn’t stand to be left alone, who pulled cushions off the couch and howled when he was stuck outside, tied up with a rope.
Karolina, soft-spoken but eager, chimed in with the next sentence:
“Getting left behind probably made his heart feel empty.”
The group had just spent 30 minutes practicing English phrases to refill prescriptions or get their test results from the doctor’s office. The story of a girl and her dog offered a welcome break.
Karolina, a Ukrainian mother of three, has spent hours reading “Because of Winn-Dixie.” Outside of class, she reads it with her kids. English has already become a regular facet of their life: They picked up the language quickly in school and chatter with their friends without issue. For children, language is a gift. For adults, it’s a challenge.
The 31-year-old is one of the more than 2,500 Ukrainians resettled in Nebraska since Russia’s invasion in February 2022.
But despite vocal support from Nebraska officials, their future remains shaky. The two paths Ukrainians used to come to the U.S. legally offer no direct path to citizenship and could be ended by the president with little notice. If they’re canceled, Ukrainians could face deportation back to a war zone.
For now, the two Ukrainian families, and 40 others, make their homes inside a cluster of three-story, beige-and-brick apartment buildings that sit a short walk from Elkhorn’s main drag. At Elk Hills, this 216-unit apartment complex, roughly 1 in 5 tenants are Ukrainian.
It’s here that they watch international news with bated breath, praying for an end to the conflict that turned their lives upside down. It’s here they have gained — and lost — government help. It’s where they have found a new sense of community, bolstered by a network of Nebraskans helping them navigate life in the U.S.
Kathy McCormack taught Russian for years, and helped several families resettle in Nebraska. Now, she teaches Karolina and her neighbors English two days a week, gathered inside the complex’s clubhouse.
Varvara is the best cook McCormack has ever met; her golubtsi, cabbage rolls stuffed with ground beef and baked in tomato sauce, have the perfect amount of dill. Karolina juggles taking care of her three children and supporting her husband, who has multiple sclerosis and uses a wheelchair. She’s planning to take English classes at Metropolitan Community College in the spring. She is the strongest woman her tutor knows.
A new resident is set to join the complex in December, bringing a baby with her. Already, the ragtag group coordinated via WhatsApp chats to proffer a travel crib and clothes for the incoming youngest member of their community.
Escaping war was the first challenge McCormack’s Ukrainian students faced. Then came immigration meetings, learning a new language and culture, finding basics like transportation, housing, a job — building a new life from scratch.
“They’re Nebraskans who were born in a different country,” McCormack said, tears welling in her eyes. “You’re not better people than they are. You’re just more fortunate.”
Oleksandr Babishkevych asks a question during an English lesson with Kathy McCormack at Elk Hills Apartments in the Elkhorn area. In class, they practice how to refill a prescription, or get test results from their doctor’s office. (Photo by Lily Smith/Flatwater Free Press)
Lynnsey Danker didn’t set out to create a Ukrainian safe harbor in the Omaha suburbs.
It was 2013, and the property manager was learning the tools of the trade from her grandfather. They were building what would become Elk Hills. That’s when they met two Ukrainian brothers, hired as subcontractors to install entryway tile.
“I’ll never forget (my grandfather) coming into the office every day and saying, ‘These two brothers are the hardest-working subcontractors that we have on site. They show up before everybody. They’re educated in their trade. They’re very professional, and they just want to talk and tell their story,’” Danker said.
Over the years, Danker lost touch with the men. In February 2022, her grandfather died. A week later, Russia invaded Ukraine. She wondered how the brothers were faring. Two months later, one of them, Nikolay, walked back into her life, this time with a request.
Four Ukrainian families were staying in his basement, he explained. They had fled the war, and while he was eager to help, his basement was full. He’d come back to the same complex he had helped build to ask Danker: Can you help newly arriving Ukrainians find a place to call home?
“It’s a ‘be kind to your neighbor’ type of situation,” she said. “I’ve got a demographic that needs a place to live, and that’s a service I can offer … The easiest thing to be is a nice human being and a nice person. And if we have something that we can offer, why wouldn’t we?”
At the outset, most Ukrainians settling in Elk Hills knew each other. Nikolay’s parents moved into the complex, as did one of his best friends — Karolina’s husband. As word spread, more Ukrainians began to flock to the apartments.
McCormack recalled helping a woman with immigration paperwork only to realize she had the same last name as another tenant. She connected the two, who discovered they were second cousins. They had never met in Ukraine; it was Elk Hills that brought them together.
At one point, as many as 60 Ukrainian families lived there.
Danker has watched her tenants put down roots. They have started working for Nebraska companies. They have joined churches and enrolled their children in local schools. She has seen those kids grow and thrive, alongside her own, and celebrated their accomplishments, like making varsity soccer.
She has seen Ukrainians meet and fall in love with American citizens, moving out on their own.
Those are the happy departures. She has seen the darker ones, too. Families whose work permits expired, waiting months for a renewal that didn’t come. Families who would rather roll the dice and go to another country, hoping for an end to their legal limbo.
Karolina Ohnivchuk prepares nalysnyky, a Ukrainian sweet crepe, at home at Elk Hills Apartments. Karolina plans to take more advanced English classes at Metropolitan Community College in the spring. (Photo by Lily Smith/Flatwater Free Press)
“We see these residents who want to work, who want to pay taxes, who want to contribute to our economy, have this taken away from them,” she said. “They can’t work, can’t pay rent, can’t support their family, can’t shop.”
In early October, the apartment-dwellers anxiously waited as the federal government considered their fate. Many Ukrainians live in the U.S. with Temporary Protected Status, which protects against deportation and allows them to work. The deadline to extend this status for Ukrainians was Oct. 19, and it remained unclear whether U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration had any appetite to do so.
Since being re-elected, Trump has canceled TPS status for 13 countries, affecting about 1 million people. While Ukrainians have for years garnered Republican sympathies and support, the relationship between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has deteriorated.
Nebraska lawmakers have tried to help where they can. In 2023, the Legislature passed a law allowing Ukrainians driver’s licenses after advocates noted an inability to drive worsened an already difficult situation for newcomers.
Gov. Jim Pillen has called Ukraine the frontline of freedom in the world. Former state lawmaker Tom Brewer has traveled to the country nine times since the war began. But much of what complicates life for Ukrainians living in Nebraska is out of the state’s control.
Speaking to a conference of advocates in Omaha Oct. 9, outgoing U.S. Rep. Don Bacon promised to push the White House hard to extend Ukrainians’ status. He extended his phone, taking a selfie with attendees to show the federal government just how much support Nebraskans had for extending TPS. But he made it clear he doesn’t believe another extension is enough.
“I really would like to see a plan for green cards and allow people to stay here permanently,” Bacon said to the crowd. “That’s the ultimate answer. It’s creating a lot of uncertainty for people … Do I buy a car? Do I buy a house? Do I put a down payment on a house? Do I have another child? All these questions are hard if you don’t have certainty, and I would sure like to create that certainty.”
Oct. 19 came and went. Instead of making a final decision, the administration posted 31 words on the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services website:
ALERT: An announcement on Ukraine’s TPS will be made at the appropriate time. Until such announcement is made, Ukrainian individuals present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection including work authorization.
Varvara laid out ingredients for the pirozhki, bowls clattering on the counter. She fetched the dough, prepared hours in advance, and got to work.
An untrained Nebraskan eye might mistake her creations for Runzas, or bierocks. But pirozhki are a cousin of the popular German pastry, Varvara, 70, explained. They can be sweet, filled with apples and butter, or savory, with minced meat and cabbage.
Varvara’s daughter and son-in-law are Canadian citizens, though they work and own a home in Omaha. When the war began, Varvara and Oleksandr decided to join the daughter and son-in-law in the U.S. They fled to Poland first, where they stayed with fellow Christians for 10 days. Then they flew to Germany, then Mexico City, where they sheltered with more believers overnight.
They didn’t know the language, where they were going, or what would happen, said the 72-year-old Oleksandr through an interpreter.
“You arrive in Mexico and you’re not sure that they aren’t going to tell you, ‘Get out of here. Go back where you came from,’” he said.
They flew to San Diego, then Omaha. For a year, they lived with their daughter and her family, but with three grandchildren already in the home, it was crowded. Then they heard about Elk Hills.
They have made the space their own. Varvara’s handmade quilted pillows decorate the apartment, and family photos are affixed proudly to their refrigerator. They take walks around the complex with their fellow countrymen in the evening, and share Varvara’s pirozhki — a small taste of home.
Varvara Babishkevych prepares pirozhki, similar to a bierock, at home at Elk Hills Apartments. Varvara often shares home-cooked Ukrainian food with neighbors. (Photo by Lily Smith/Flatwater Free Press)
Varvara and Oleksandr miss Ukraine. But the small city they lived in has been a target for attacks. Returning would be a death wish.
At the same time, living in the U.S. is becoming tougher for the couple. Oleksandr has circulation issues in his legs that have required multiple surgeries to fix. After a heart surgery in Kyiv in 2020, the retiree is cautious about his health.
This fall he, like thousands of other non-citizens, lost Medicaid when federal eligibility changes went into effect. He has enough of his blood thinner medication to make it to Christmas, but isn’t sure what he’ll do after. Without a green card, they no longer get Medicaid or SNAP benefits.
Karolina’s family feels the same strain. Before his illness, her husband built furniture in Ukraine, and she volunteered helping special needs and disadvantaged kids. The couple would visit homes to spread the gospel, and help intervene if, say, a husband had an alcohol problem.
Lines of scripture decorate their American apartment’s walls. Through love, serve one another.
Now, her husband’s illness keeps him from working. His medical needs are no longer covered by Medicaid.
Her husband, Sasha, asked her: “How can you love me in this condition?” Her reply was simple, he said.
Sasha sees their presence in the U.S. and the support they have found as a sign of God’s grace. They also desperately miss home. But their kids have built a life here, and any decision to go back to Ukraine would need to take them into account.
In January, Karolina will begin her college English courses. She doesn’t know how long they will be in the U.S., but she knows she wants to be competent, for her children’s sake.
She has dog-eared her copy of “Because of Winn-Dixie,” a reader habit with no direct translation in her native language. She’s starting to learn more advanced phrases in English under McCormack’s patient tutelage.
Descriptive language in this story of a girl and her dog, phrases like “snuffled his nose on her little old-lady feet,” have begun to be more than just words on the page. They have started to make sense.
The class closes the book at the end of Chapter 6. Be ready to read Chapter 7 next week, McCormack says in English, and have a good weekend, she says in Russian. She, like her pupils, doesn’t know what the future holds. But she’s ready to help, for as long as she can.
“There’s a fire out there,” McCormack said. “Do you try to put it out, or do you turn your back?”

US MARKETS CALL: S&P 500 Valuation Dives As Earnings Soar
The stock market dived last week. Investors priced in political backlash against data centers after Democrats swept Congress. We anticipated buying opportunities after the midterm elections, and Thursday’s selloff delivered some. This remains an earnings-led bull market. Valuations are falling while earnings are soaring. We still view the AI backlash as another speed bump, not a roadblock. We are sticking with our 7,900 year-end target for the S&P 500.
The Nasdaq entered correction territory on Thursday and closed the week below its 200-day moving average (chart). It has done this before recently. It rebounded sharply after its Spring 2025 "Liberation Day" plunge and again after the Iran war started earlier this year, quickly resuming its uptrend both times.
The equal-weight S&P 500 is holding up remarkably well. It remains near its recent record high and above both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages (chart). The damage has been concentrated in the AI trade, not the broader market.
The Magnificent-7 are underperforming again. The MAGS ETF is up only 2.4% ytd, versus 7.8% for the S&P 500 (chart). The Impressive-493 also took a hit this week. The XMAGS ETF includes Micron and the other semiconductor stocks hit hardest in the selloff. It is still up 10.0% ytd.
Dow Theory remains bullish. The Dow Jones Industrial Average is holding up well near its highs (chart). The Transports have lagged. They should improve if oil prices continue to fall.
Earnings season picked up this week. The blended Q3 S&P 500 EPS growth estimate (i.e., actual results for companies that have reported, estimates for those that haven’t yet) rose to 25.9% y/y from 23.8% a week earlier, helped by AMD’s solid results. Q4’s estimate edged down to 29.7% (chart). As we noted previously, Q2’s 50.4% y/y EPS growth rate was boosted by mark-to-market gains at Alphabet and Amazon. Excluding those, growth was closer to 25%, which is still very strong.
Forward earnings rose to a record $418.25. It is converging on the 2027 estimate of $426.28, which continues to climb (chart). Analysts’ 2028 consensus S&P 500 EPS estimate rose to $495.14; it’s been closing in on $500—which is our target for 2030! We are bullish, but not as bullish as the analysts. The drop in the forward P/E this year suggests that investors also believe analysts are too bullish on earnings.
Forward earnings for the S&P 500, S&P 400, and S&P 600 all rose to record highs again last week (chart). Earnings strength remains broad.
S&P 500 forward revenues per share is up 15.9% y/y, while forward earnings per share is up 39.0% y/y (chart).
The S&P 500 forward P/E fell to 17.6 last week, below the 2025 Liberation Day low (chart). P/E plunges typically accompany corrections and recessions. The economy shows no sign of a recession anytime soon. Investors instead fear irrational exuberance in earnings forecasts.
Since the bull market began on October 12, 2022, the S&P 500 has risen 106.2%. Forward earnings is up 75.5%, while the forward P/E is up 22.5% (chart). The P/E and E both drove the rally until the forward P/E peaked in October last year. Since then, E has done all the work. Investors are finding it harder to predict the return on all the AI capital spending. They won’t pay an excessive multiple given that uncertainty.
The S&P 500 Semiconductors industry accounts for much of the P/E drop. The industry index's forward P/E has plunged to 13.1, well below the S&P 500’s (chart). Semis are now cheaper than they were during the 2022 bear market.
The futures market expects about two rate hikes over the next 12 months. That explains why the 2-year Treasury yield remains well above the 3.88% federal funds rate, even after easing to 4.46% following the midterms (chart).
The 10-year Treasury yield continues to fall. It dropped to 4.84% and is testing its uptrend line from last year’s low (chart). We’ll see if it bounces. Either way, it is back in the 4.00%-5.00% “old normal” range where we feel comfortable.
The 10-year TIPS yield fell to 2.62%. The yield spread between the 10-year Treasury and TIPS, a widely used proxy for expected inflation, eased to 2.22% (chart). That proxy tends to move with oil prices. The recent drop in crude showed up here.
The price of Brent crude oil fell to $98.32 a barrel in recent days (chart). No news of the re-escalation of the war in the Middle East has emerged since the midterms. Hopes for a US-Iran deal are reflected in the oil market. We still see a risk of re-escalation.
Nearby gasoline futures dropped to $2.78 a gallon last week (chart). If sustained, that should start to show up as lower inflation in a couple of months. Renewed fighting in the Middle East would reverse that.
Steel prices show no sign of a slowdown in data center construction. US Midwest hot-rolled coil rose to $1,357 a ton, the highest since 2022 (chart).
Agricultural prices have eased. The S&P GSCI Agriculture Spot index fell to 376.77 last week (chart). Fears of a food price spike should subside.

items.title: US offers millions for information on Iran’s nuclear program despite Trump’s claims of obliteration - CNN
items.summary: US offers millions for information on Iran’s nuclear program despite Trump’s claims of obliteration  CNN
items.content:
The US is offering a multi-million-dollar reward for information it might be able to use to eradicate Iran's nuclear program - the same nuclear program Trump has repeatedly claimed to have ended.
The United States is offering a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran’s nuclear program, despite US President Donald Trump’s repeated claims to have obliterated Tehran’s capabilities.
Rewards for Justice (RFJ), a State Department program, is seeking tips on Iran’s nuclear facilities, equipment and associated personnel, the program said in a Friday social media post, which stated that relocation may be offered to informants.
During the 12-day conflict last year, Trump was quick to declare that Iran’s key nuclear enrichment facilities had been “completely and totally obliterated.” He kept up this assessment on several occasions after and attacked media organizations — including CNN — for challenging the claim.
This year’s conflict saw the US and Israel again attack Iranian nuclear sites, and Trump has made fresh claims to have tackled Iran’s threat, telling reporters on Friday that “if we didn’t hit Iran, you wouldn’t have Israel today.”
But the State Department’s move — and independent assessments — suggest that concerns remain over Iran’s program, which Tehran has always insisted is peaceful.
Last year, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) reported that Iran was enriching uranium to 60% purity which is “a short technical step from the 90% required for a nuclear weapon,” according to an RFJ statement.
“Iran is the only non-nuclear-weapon state to produce uranium at such a high enrichment level. Experts estimate this quantity, if enriched further, could be enough for several nuclear weapons,” it said.
It also referred to a “loss of continuity of knowledge regarding Iran’s production and inventory of key components like centrifuges” due to the regime’s lack of compliance with the IAEA.
Preventing Iran from developing a nuclear weapon has been stated as a key objective for Washington’s war with Iran. This week, President Donald Trump repeated claims that the US “might have to go after” Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, the suspected underground nuclear site where Israel believes Tehran has stored part of its enriched uranium stockpile and advanced enrichment centrifuges.
In response, Iran warned that any US attack on Iranian nuclear facilities would be treated as an expansion of the war in the region. Tehran maintains that it has the right to develop nuclear energy for peaceful purposes, including enrichment.
RFJ has also offered rewards for information on senior Iranian regime figures since the war began in February.
Women hold placards critical of U.S. President Donald Trump during an anti-U.S. rally in Tehran on Nov. 4, 2026, a day after the U.S. midterm elections. (Kyodo via AP Images) ==Kyodo
Iran’s hardliners see a weakened Trump – and want more to end the war
Mediators are continuing to try to broker an agreement between Iran and the US, but both sides appear unwilling to shift on key red lines, with Tehran seeing the ability to enrich uranium as a matter of national sovereignty.
Trump ordered new strikes on Iran overnight, describing them as “minor.”
Explosions were heard on Iran’s Qeshm Island and in the southern Iranian port of Jask, Reuters reported on Saturday, citing Iranian media.
Iran has not officially confirmed the source ⁠of the reported explosions, according to Reuters.
Earlier on Saturday, Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency said two missiles had struck Qeshm Island, with no ‌official information on ⁠potential damage. But later that evening Tasnim cited an Iranian source as saying that the explosions heard on the Island were not related ⁠to missile strikes.
In a separate development, CENTCOM has launched a task force with the intention of preventing Iran from accessing land routes that might facilitate the transportation of advanced weapons and other materials.
A naval blockade is already in place as part of US efforts to choke off Iran’s vital oil industry.
